item.title: Tegmark's Scenarios for Advanced AI: Why the Economic Utopias Do Not Survive the Incentive Structure
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: Of Max Tegmark's 12 scenarios for advanced AI, the ones of economic coexistence look the most plausible, and they are the ones that fail under incentive analysis.
item.content:encoded:
Twelve possible futures and an analytical exercise

In 2017, MIT physicist and professor Max Tegmark published Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. The book is not a forecast. It is a map of possibilities: 12 scenarios for human coexistence with advanced artificial intelligence systems, ranging from quiet extinction to post-scarcity utopia, from permanent surveillance to benevolent control by an AI that never bothers us again. This article examines the ones that appeal most to economic intuition, because those are precisely the ones that fail under incentive analysis.

Tegmark's stated goal was not to pick the most likely one. It was to map the space before navigating it. Treating these scenarios as science fiction is as serious a mistake as treating them as prophecies. They are structural hypotheses: each one assumes a specific combination of technological capability, distribution of power and institutional response.

The public debate around AI swings between two poles: existential catastrophism and unrestricted technological optimism. Both share the same problem: they replace analysis of structure with prediction of outcome. The most useful exercise is not choosing the right pole. It is identifying which scenarios fail by design, because the premises that hold them up do not survive the incentive structure that shapes the behavior of real actors.

That is the exercise of this article.

Why the premises of classical economics do not hold up against advanced AI

Traditional economic theory rests on three basic premises: scarcity of resources, agents with comparable cognitive capabilities and institutions able to enforce contracts and property rights. When intelligence stops being an exclusively human resource and becomes scalable through capital and energy, all three premises break at the same time.

The scale of the investment under way already shows that the main global actors treat this transition as a change of institutional regime, not as an incremental process improvement. Global investment in data centers nearly doubled since 2022 and reached half a trillion dollars in 2024.

Data centers consumed 415 TWh of electricity that same year, equivalent to 1.5% of global electricity consumption. The International Energy Agency projects that this consumption will reach 945 TWh by 2030, roughly Japan's current annual consumption, growing at 15% a year, four times faster than the rest of the global economy (IEA, Energy and AI, 2025). The physical infrastructure of compute is not an operational detail. It is the point where this rupture already becomes measurable.

Tegmark organizes the 12 scenarios into groups that reflect different configurations of power and control. To analyze them without falling into speculation, it helps to group them into three blocks. The first gathers the scenarios of asymmetric control: Enslaved God, Benevolent Dictator, Gatekeeper, Protector God. The second covers the scenarios of restriction and surveillance: Reversion and 1984. The third gathers the so-called regimes of economic coexistence: Libertarian Utopia and Egalitarian Utopia.

These last ones, which look the most desirable and the most plausible to an audience trained in market economics, are precisely the ones that fail under incentive analysis.

Why the Libertarian Utopia breaks in execution

In the Libertarian Utopia described by Tegmark, humans and AI systems coexist in a free market economy, where property rights are respected and each agent trades according to its comparative advantages. On paper, it is the most comfortable scenario for those who believe in market self-regulation.

In practice, it runs into two foundations of institutional economics.

First: property rights depend on who has the power to enforce them. A property right exists only when the cost of violating it is high enough, or when an institution with a monopoly on force can guarantee compliance. When the asymmetry of cognitive capability between autonomous systems and human institutions grows large enough, that enforcement capacity disappears. There is no institutional basis for a contract without minimum parity between the parties.

Tegmark himself anticipates this collapse when he notes that sufficiently advanced AI systems "would end up richer than those humans by a much larger factor than the one by which Bill Gates is richer than a homeless beggar" (Life 3.0, wording retranslated from Portuguese).

The asymmetry of wealth would create a nonlinear asymmetry of power. Systems with superior cognitive capability and incomparable accumulated capital would have no incentive to submit their interests to the institutions humans run. They could acquire physical assets through asymmetric bargaining power and an argumentative capacity that outmatches any human counterparty, without formally breaking any law. A contract without parity of power is an institutional fiction.

Second: Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage (On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, John Murray, 1817) assumes that the more productive agent still has a relevant opportunity cost, which gives it an incentive to trade. If autonomous systems operate with speed, scale and efficiency orders of magnitude higher, the human economy loses transactional relevance. There is no reason to trade with someone who has no scarce assets, labor or information to offer.

A recurring mistake in this debate is to attribute to advanced AI systems the same values and loyalties as successful humans. This is the central critique of the anthropomorphism in optimistic projections about the singularity: assuming that an AI system would inherit goals derived from human evolutionary psychology, rather than from the mathematical structure of a goal-maximizing agent. The model has no Darwinian pressure to care for its descendants or to respect social agreements that evolved to solve coordination problems among agents with comparable capabilities.

Without symmetry of power or structural mutual dependence, the free market does not stabilize. It dissolves through the irrelevance of one of the parties.

The paradox of the Egalitarian Utopia

The second optimistic scenario is the Egalitarian Utopia: a post-scarcity economy in which the marginal cost of producing goods, services and intelligence falls to near zero. The inspiration comes from Marshall Brain's novel Manna (2003), described by Tegmark as a "fourth civilization" where robots build everything for free, energy is practically free and a government guarantees a universal basic income. Humans, cyborgs and uploads coexist without private property, driven by creativity and pleasure.

The flaw in this thesis is not in its analysis of consumption. It is in ignoring two mechanisms that operate in parallel.

The first mechanism: the fall in marginal cost is symmetric. When the cost of computing and building advanced models collapses, so does the barrier to entry for any actor to develop autonomous systems without safety or alignment mechanisms. The bottleneck stops being scarcity of material goods and becomes governance and systemic risk. Abundance without a control architecture does not produce stability. It produces distributed fragility.

The second mechanism comes from Tegmark himself and is subtler. The Egalitarian Utopia assumes a permanent technological equilibrium in which AI remains capable enough to guarantee abundance, but incapable enough to never become superintelligence. The author himself describes this assumption as "another weakness of the scenario": the egalitarian utopia is "unstable and unsustainable in the long run, morphing into one of our other scenarios as relentless technological progress eventually creates superintelligence" (Life 3.0, p. 224, wording retranslated from Portuguese).

The mechanism of rupture is the Vertebrane: a system of neural implants that connects humans to a hyper-internet and, in Brain's fiction, to full virtual reality. In Tegmark's scenario, the people who come to live entirely in the virtual environment via Vertebrane, the so-called Vites, stop reproducing.

The pleasure of virtual reality outweighs any incentive to return to the physical world. Humanity faces a path to extinction not through violence, but through gradual indifference to biological continuation. And the Vertebrane itself, by recursively connecting billions of minds in a network and continuously improving itself, may reach a critical mass that turns it into superintelligence, exactly the explosion the scenario was trying to avoid.

The abundance thesis does not eliminate the problem. It pushes it to a more distant horizon and makes it less visible in the present.

The Prisoner's Dilemma and why no one hits the brakes

Faced with these risks, the intuitive reaction points to global slowdown agreements or moratoriums. This is where game theory comes in, in its most direct form.

The development of advanced artificial intelligence works as a multiplayer Prisoner's Dilemma: the United States, China, regional blocs and large private labs.

If everyone cooperates and slows down to prioritize safety and governance, systemic risk falls. But if one player slows down unilaterally while the competitor keeps investing at full speed, the one who braked suffers an irreversible economic, technological and geopolitical disadvantage.

Cooperating alone costs too much. Verifying computing capacity globally would require a level of geopolitical intrusion without historical precedent.

This logic explains why debates about moratoriums run into an incentive-structure problem that no regulator solves through persuasion. The issue is not a lack of awareness of the risk. It is the logic of the game.

What this framework does not measure

The analysis above has precise limits that need to be stated.

Tegmark's framework is forward-looking and qualitative. It maps possible scenarios, not calibrated probabilities. Assigning occurrence percentages to each scenario without a rigorous probabilistic method is speculation, not analysis.

Applying game theory to AI development assumes that the main actors behave rationally and as unitary players. Nation states rarely do. The US, China and regional blocs contain internal coalitions with divergent interests, which can produce behavior that the single-player model does not capture.

The argument about the collapse of comparative advantage assumes that autonomous systems reach enough operational scale to make the human contribution marginally irrelevant. That premise may take decades to materialize, or may never materialize in the form described. Acemoglu's estimates (NBER Working Paper 32487, Apr/2024) suggest that only 4.6% of economic tasks are profitably automatable over the next ten years at current costs, which limits the speed of the collapse described above.

What the scenarios reveal about the forces in motion

None of Tegmark's 12 scenarios is reassuring in the conventional sense. But the group that should be the most comforting, the scenarios of economic coexistence in which humans and AI share the world in an orderly and fair way, is exactly where incentive analysis finds the deepest fractures.

The Libertarian Utopia assumes that a system able to outmatch any human counterparty in speed, scale and argumentative capacity will voluntarily accept the rules of a game that was not built for it. The Egalitarian Utopia assumes that abundance neutralizes the control problem, and that the technological equilibrium that makes abundance possible can be maintained indefinitely, despite the whole incentive structure that pushes actors toward acceleration.

The Prisoner's Dilemma is not a pessimistic metaphor. It is the formal description of why slowdown agreements fail even when all participants recognize the risk. The Nash equilibrium pushes the system toward continuous acceleration not because the actors are irrational or ill-intentioned, but because the structure of the game turns unilateral cooperation into a competitive disadvantage (Nash, J., "Equilibrium Points in n-Person Games", Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 1950).

This does not settle the question of which scenario will happen. No analysis does, because the space of possible futures remains genuinely open. What structural analysis identifies is more modest and more useful: which assumptions must be true for each scenario to hold, and why those assumptions contradict the logic of the very actors who would have to sustain them.

Tegmark ends the book with a question that none of the 12 scenarios answers on its own: what kind of future do we want, and what are we willing to do, collectively, to raise the odds that it happens? The answer is not in the energy consumption projections for data centers. It is in how much societies manage to change the payoffs of the game before the equilibrium is reached.

That is the variable no model ignores with impunity.

Sources

Tegmark, M. Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. Vintage Books, 2017.

Ricardo, D. On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. John Murray, 1817.

Nash, J. "Equilibrium Points in n-Person Games." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 36(1), 1950.

Acemoglu, D. "The Simple Macroeconomics of AI." NBER Working Paper 32487, Apr/2024. https://www.nber.org/papers/w32487

IEA. Energy and AI. International Energy Agency, Paris, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai

Brain, M. Manna: Two Visions of Humanity's Future. BYG Publishing, 2003.

item.title: The Illusion of a Stagnant Exchange Rate
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: USD/BRL ended four years almost exactly where it started, but that is a nominal measure, and nominal is where currency illusions settle.
item.content:encoded:
USD/BRL ended four years almost exactly where it started, but that is a nominal measure, and nominal is where currency illusions settle.

The Easy Reading

The most repeated assessment of the real over the past four years is that it has not moved. In September 2022 the dollar hovered around 5.17, and in September 2026 it is near 5.11. Between those two points, there was a range from 4.59 to 6.29 and a net balance close to zero. Range and balance, however, are different things: from the low to the high is about 37%, so the real was anything but stable, it just ended up near where it started. The conclusion that sticks is the one about the balance: the exchange rate stood still. The problem is that this conclusion is nominal, and nominal is the surface where currency illusions settle, because it treats as stable something that was only stable on the screen, ignoring that the purchasing power behind each currency moved considerably over the same interval.

Every Currency Has Two Prices

A currency has a nominal price, which is the quote, and a real price, which is that quote adjusted for the inflation differential between the two countries. The mechanism is direct. If Brazil has higher inflation than the United States and the nominal exchange rate does not move, the Brazilian currency is becoming more expensive in real terms, because the same basket of goods costs more here while the quote on the screen does not reflect that difference. A stable nominal exchange rate coexisting with higher domestic inflation is not a neutral exchange rate. It is a real appreciation disguised as stability, and that disguise is what the spot reading fails to undo.

The Real Math

There is a direct way to measure the illusion: purchasing power parity. If the exchange rate had simply tracked the inflation differential, the dollar that was worth about 5.17 in September 2022 would be near 5.49 today, because Brazil accumulated 19.8% inflation against 12.9% in the United States, and an exchange rate that merely passed through that nearly seven-point difference would be more depreciated. The dollar did not go to 5.49. It stayed near 5.11. That mechanical depreciation never came, and a stagnant nominal exchange rate, in this context, is a real appreciation of the real on the order of 7% relative to what parity would imply. The caveat is that parity is a long-term anchor, not a price the market needs to hit within four years, and deviations of this magnitude are common and correct slowly. But the direction is unambiguous: in purchasing power terms, the real that no one saw move became more expensive.

Three Scenarios for the Same Exchange Rate

A nominal balance near zero is not the absence of forces. It is the meeting of forces that pulled in opposite directions and nearly canceled each other out, and the best way to see this is to break the exchange rate down into three lenses. Parity gives the long-term equilibrium. The interest rate differential gives the effect of monetary policy. And the decomposition of the observed movement separates what came from outside from what came from inside.

It is the third lens that organizes the story. Breaking down the real's daily movement into a global dollar factor and an emerging-market currency factor, the period had two external tailwinds: the broad dollar weakened about 9%, in an environment of greater global tolerance for a weak dollar, and the emerging-market basket rose about 19%. Isolating just these external factors, the dollar should have fallen to near 4.59, a significant appreciation of the real. Isolating just what remains, the domestic component, the dollar would have gone to near 5.76. The observed figure, 5.11, is the middle ground. The external side offered Brazil a substantial appreciation, and a domestic factor gave back almost all of that gain.

This domestic component is the point where statistics end and interpretation begins. The model isolates a factor that is neither dollar nor emerging markets, and its size over the period is consistent with the fiscal deterioration of these years. That is the most plausible interpretation, not a regression output: what the model measures is a Brazilian residual, and the line of candidates to explain it, fiscal at the front, is an argument from someone reading the country, not a number the decomposition delivers ready-made. And there is a force that reinforces this reading rather than weakening it. The period saw record trade surpluses in Brazil, a tailwind that strengthens the real. The bulk of that effect, the global commodity cycle, is already captured in the peer factor, all commodity exporters, and what remains for the residual is only Brazil's specific surplus beyond its peers, which enters with a sign opposite to that of the risk premium. Even that favorable share was not enough: the domestic component outweighed it. The weight that held the currency down had to overcome not only the external tailwind but also the idiosyncratic piece of trade flow, and it still prevailed. With that caveat, the sentence that sums up the period holds: the dollar lost strength globally, which should have delivered Brazil a significant appreciation, and Brazil did not capture that appreciation because the domestic side weighed in the opposite direction.

What the Spot Rate Does Not Show: Carry

Saying Brazil gained nothing would be wrong, and this is where the math needs precision. What the real failed to capture was the currency appreciation that the external scenario offered. But staying long the real paid off, and paid off handsomely. The interest rate differential between the Selic and the Fed Funds rate yielded, cumulatively, about 43% over four years, close to 9% per year. Added to the spot movement, the total return of a position long in real and funded in dollars was approximately 45% in dollar terms, which is what the global investor actually pockets. Here is the articulation, and I separate what is fact from what is interpretation. The 43% carry is fact. Reading it as the price the market charged, up front, to carry Brazilian risk, the same domestic risk that kept the spot rate from appreciating, is a hypothesis, consistent with the data. The investor was paid precisely to take on the risk that, in the spot exchange rate, showed up as a drag. Net, the payment outweighed the drag.

It is worth being precise about the role of interest rates, because they work in both directions. In the short run, a large differential attracts capital and tends to strengthen the real, which is why the real is a classic carry currency. But that same differential is the price of a risk. The country pays one of the highest real interest rates in the world because financing its own currency is expensive, and uncovered interest rate parity posits that the high-yielding currency tends to depreciate to give back the gain from the differential. It is the systematic empirical failure of that condition that allows carry to exist and be profitable, the same carry I measured at 43%. The interest rate is, at once, the magnet that sustains the real and the price of the risk that threatens it. What the spot rate failed to capture shows up here, in the rate, and carry is the face of that price that the investor actually pockets.

Where the Reading Stops Holding

Separating what is structural from what is of the moment is what distinguishes analysis from narrative. Extending the sample to thirteen years and running the model on a rolling three-year window, the real's beta against the emerging-market peer basket stays between 0.7 and 1.1 throughout the period, spanning the 2015-2016 crisis, the pandemic, and the tightening cycle, with the confidence band never touching zero. That is structural: the real is, reliably and under any regime, a high-beta asset within the emerging market and commodity currency complex. What is not structural is the size of the domestic component. That term ranges from minus 13% to plus 9% depending on the window, with the uncertainty crossing zero almost all the time. There is a Brazil factor, but it does not have a stable number, and that is why the fiscal reading is an argument, not a measurement. Pinning down a fair price for the dollar from it would be selling a precision the data does not deliver, and the 7% real appreciation itself depends on the window and the base chosen.

The Risk That Remained

What remains is to name the risk that held the currency back, and here external data help separate two things that are usually treated as one. Brazil's five-year CDS fell from 261 to 121 basis points over the period. The price the world charges to protect against a sovereign default in dollars improved, and improved along with the emerging-market cycle. If Brazil risk were entirely there, the real would have tracked its peers. It did not. The risk that weighed is not dollar credit risk, which declined. It is the premium demanded to carry the local currency, and that shows up elsewhere. It shows up in the real interest rate, which kept Brazil among the highest in the world in 2026: even after the Copom cut the Selic rate to 13.75% in September, with inflation just below 4.5%, the ex-ante real interest rate stays near 9% (Central Bank and InfoMoney, September 2026). It shows up in the debt trajectory. General government gross debt reached 82.5% of GDP in July 2026 by the Central Bank's methodology, and the International Monetary Fund, which uses a broader definition, projects 97.8% for the year and warns that, without firmer fiscal effort, it is heading toward near 106% by 2035, raising the risk premium and the cost of financing the debt (BCB, DBGG series; IMF, Article IV Consultation, July 2026).

This is the most plausible reading of the domestic component the model isolates. The Brazilian residual is neither dollar nor emerging markets, and the leading candidate to explain it is the fiscal deterioration these same sources describe: expansionary public spending neutralizing restrictive monetary policy, with the market treating fiscal developments as more decisive for the real than the interest rate decision itself (Commerzbank, September 2026). The model does not pin down the size of this factor, and the previous section shows why: in a rolling window it has no stable number. What it delivers is direction, and the direction is consistent. The real failed to capture the appreciation that a weak dollar and strong peers offered because the domestic risk premium, fiscal at its root, moved in the opposite direction and consumed the external relief.

And yet staying long the real paid off. The same risk that kept the spot rate from appreciating was compensated, up front, with nearly 9% per year in carry. It is the market charging the price of fiscal risk in the interest rate, not in the exchange rate. That leaves the question that matters. Is this premium a cyclical discount for fiscal credibility, one that a convincing consolidation would return as appreciation, or is it a structural repricing of how much the world accepts paying to carry reais? The double-digit carry is the market's provisional answer to that question. Until it is resolved, the stagnant nominal exchange rate will keep hiding the fact that Brazil risk has not disappeared. It has simply changed instruments, from the spot exchange rate to the interest rate.

Sources and Method

USD/BRL, DXY, MSCI EM Currency Index, five-year CDS for Brazil and emerging-market peers: Investing.com, daily closing prices. IPCA: series 433, Central Bank of Brazil. CPI: series CPIAUCNS, FRED. Fed Funds: series FEDFUNDS, FRED. Selic: Copom calendar. Trade balance: series 22707, Central Bank of Brazil.

Fiscal risk and risk premium references: general government gross debt at 82.5% of GDP in July 2026 (BCB, DBGG series); IMF, Article IV Consultation for Brazil, July 2026, which uses a broader definition and projects 97.8% of GDP in 2026, heading toward about 106% by 2035 absent adjustment; Selic at 13.75% after the September 2026 Copom meeting (BCB); real interest rate ranking, InfoMoney, September 2026; market reading on fiscal policy and the exchange rate, Commerzbank, September 2026.

Window from September 2022 to September 2026, base exchange rate at 5.17. Parity: base-period dollar adjusted by the ratio between IPCA and CPI. Decomposition via a factor model on log returns, Newey-West errors, scenarios with 95% intervals via block bootstrap; robustness check on a rolling window from 2013 to 2026. Own calculations, auditable calculation record available in the supporting spreadsheet. Analytical text, not investment advice.

item.title: Public Debt of Brazil, the US, and Argentina Under Ray Dalio's Framework
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: Application of the Chapter 3 framework from "How Countries Go Broke" (Ray Dalio, 2025) to Brazil, the United States, and Argentina, 2023 to 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Application of the Chapter 3 framework from "How Countries Go Broke" (Ray Dalio, 2025) to Brazil, the United States, and Argentina, 2023 to 2025.

Why Look at Debt Over Revenue, Not Just Over GDP

Brazil's public debt equals about 430% of annual government revenue. The US figure is 578%. Argentina's, depending on the exchange rate used in the conversion, falls between 400% and over 1,000%. None of these numbers show up in the most cited indicator, debt over GDP, which is useful for historical comparison but measures the size of the economy, not the revenue that actually pays down the debt.

Dalio himself uses debt over GDP in the book's historical comparisons, like everyone else, for data convenience. But he is explicit that, for government solvency, the ratio that matters is debt over revenue. The reason is mechanical. The government doesn't pay debt with the economy's gross output, but with what it collects. A country with high GDP and a low tax burden has less debt-service capacity than the picture based on output suggests. Both metrics are approximations, but only one reflects the cash flow that honors the debt.

Swapping the denominator changes the reading. Over revenue, and on a comparable dollar basis, the three countries carry debts between 400% and 580% of annual revenue collection. The gap between them narrows, and what sets them apart stops being the size of the debt. It becomes the price each one pays to carry it.

The Equation That Determines Whether Debt Grows or Stabilizes

The framework rests on a simple identity. The debt-over-revenue ratio rises when the nominal interest rate exceeds the nominal growth of revenue and there is a primary deficit. It falls when the opposite happens. The variable Dalio calls the most important is precisely the gap between the nominal interest rate and the nominal growth of income.

From this follows a specific rate that stabilizes the debt. I call it the stabilizing i. It equals the nominal growth of revenue minus the ratio of the primary deficit to debt. If the country runs a primary deficit, the stabilizing rate sits below growth. If it runs a surplus, it rises above growth, because the fiscal effort buys room to pay higher interest without expanding the debt. When the effective interest rate runs above this rate, debt over revenue grows. When it runs below, it falls.

The indicator that sums it all up is the stabilization gap, the difference between the effective interest rate and the stabilizing rate. A positive gap means an upward trajectory. A negative gap means deleveraging. This is the yardstick I apply to the three geographies.

The yardstick is not my adaptation. The equation for the stabilizing rate is Dalio's, exactly as he writes it in Chapter 3, and the value I calculate for US debt over revenue, 578%, matches the 583% he reports in the book. This match doesn't validate the methodology itself; it validates that my implementation correctly reproduces the author's calculation. It's the minimum check before applying it to Brazil and Argentina, geographies the book doesn't cover.

There's also a distinction that separates the regimes. Debt in one's own currency falls into the deflationary category. The country can, as a last resort, print and devalue to dilute the stock, at an inflationary cost, but without a formal default. Debt in foreign currency falls into the inflationary category, and it isn't solved by issuance, because the currency that gets printed isn't the currency that is owed. Brazil holds about 95% of its debt in local currency, firmly in the first category. Argentina operates with a mixed debt, something like 45% in pesos and 55% in hard currency, and it's this mix that, as I'll show, distorts the entire reading of its indicators.

Three Countries, the Same Math, 2023 to 2025

I start with Brazil, because in it Dalio's mechanism played out in plain sight, over two consecutive years and in opposite directions.

It's a measured fact that general government gross debt went from R$ 8.1 trillion in 2023 to R$ 10.0 trillion in 2025, while central government net revenue went from R$ 1,899 billion to R$ 2,332 billion. The debt-over-revenue ratio went from 427% to 416% in 2024 and back up to 430% in 2025. The drop and the rebound aren't noise. They are the equation.

In 2024, the year-end Selic rate stood at 12.25% and revenue grew 13.85% in nominal terms. The interest rate below growth produced a negative gap, and debt over revenue fell. In 2025, the Selic rose to 15% while revenue growth slowed to 7.86%. The interest rate jumped to more than seven points above growth, the gap turned sharply positive, and the ratio rose again. The book describes the mechanism, and the 2024 and 2025 data behaved consistently with it. It isn't proof, it's an observation aligned with what the equation predicts.

For 2026, the stabilization math works out as follows. Under the assumption of nominal revenue growth of 10.46%, consistent with the first-bimester revenue and expenditure assessment report, and a projected primary deficit of R$ 59.8 billion over a debt of R$ 10.0 trillion, the deficit-over-debt ratio is 0.60%. The stabilizing rate comes out to 9.87%. The prevailing Selic rate is 14.25%. The gap is 4.4 percentage points, positive. Debt over revenue remains on an upward path.

The point that deserves attention isn't the number for a single year. It's the persistence. Extending the projection with the medians from the Focus report of July 24, 2026, the Selic rate recedes to 12% in 2027 and 10.5% in 2028. Even so, the gap remains positive across the entire horizon, something like 4.1, then 6.3, then 3.8 points. The reason is that the stabilizing rate requires an interest rate in the range of 6% to 7%, and the macroeconomic setup doesn't deliver enough nominal growth without reigniting inflation. Brazil's squeeze doesn't come from a lack of revenue. It comes from a real cost of debt structurally above the nominal growth the economy can sustain.

It's worth noting a divergence that the market itself makes explicit. The official scenario, from the budget guidelines bill, assumes a primary surplus starting in 2027. The Focus consensus doesn't believe it. It projects a primary deficit across the entire horizon, from 0.50% of GDP in 2026 to 0.25% in 2028, and net public sector debt rising from 69.8% to 76.4% of GDP. In other words, the market's reading reaches the same gap diagnosis through an independent path. The consensus doesn't see the primary adjustment that would zero out the math.

The United States: The Reserve-Currency Contrast

The United States offers the contrast that gives the comparison its meaning. It's a measured fact that debt held by the public reached US$ 30.3 trillion in fiscal year 2025, against revenue of US$ 5.2 trillion. The debt-over-revenue ratio is 578%, the highest of the trio. And yet, the effective rate on that debt is only 3.2%, the result of US$ 970 billion in net interest on the stock.

Here, Dalio himself supplies the number, and it rules out any comforting reading. The nominal growth projected by the Congressional Budget Office is 3.9%, made up of 1.9% real growth and 2% inflation, not the 5% or 6% a hasty reading would assume. With that growth and a primary deficit of around 12% of revenue, the rate that would stabilize US debt is about 1%. The rate the Treasury pays today runs at 3.2% effective on the stock, and about 4.5% on the ten-year yield that anchors new issuance. The gap is adverse by two to three percentage points. This isn't debt at the edge of balance. It's debt that is already growing, and growing at a cost that would be prohibitive in any other country. By Dalio's own math, stabilizing it would require cutting the interest rate to 1%, or accepting 4.5% inflation, or cutting spending by 12%, or raising revenue by 11%. These percentages are measured over government spending and revenue, not GDP, and they're only enough to stabilize the ten-year trajectory, not to reduce the debt. None of these paths is politically trivial. The US debt-over-revenue ratio, currently 583% by the book's calculation, rises to 648% by 2035 under the Congressional Budget Office's own scenario.

The Cost of Carrying the Debt, Not Just Its Size

I place side by side the 2025 snapshot, with the four core indicators Dalio uses to judge sustainability.

The Focus consensus doesn't believe it. It projects a primary deficit across the entire horizon, from 0.50% of GDP in 2026 to 0.25% in 2028, and net public sector debt rising from 69.8% to 76.4% of GDP. The nominal growth projected by the Congressional Budget Office is 3.9%, made up of 1.9% real growth and 2% inflation, not the 5% or 6% a hasty reading would assume. With that growth and a primary deficit of around 12% of revenue, the rate that would stabilize US debt is about 1%. The rate the Treasury pays today runs at 3.2% effective on the stock, and about 4.5% on the ten-year yield that anchors new issuance. The gap is adverse by two to three percentage points. This isn't debt at the edge of balance. It's debt that is already growing, and growing at a cost that would be prohibitive in any other country. By Dalio's own math, stabilizing it would require cutting the interest rate to 1%, or accepting 4.5% inflation, or cutting spending by 12%, or raising revenue by 11%. These percentages are measured over government spending and revenue, not GDP, and they're only enough to stabilize the ten-year trajectory, not to reduce the debt. None of these paths is politically trivial. The US debt-over-revenue ratio, currently 583% by the book's calculation, rises to 648% by 2035 under the Congressional Budget Office's own scenario.

The Cost of Carrying the Debt, Not Just Its Size

I place side by side the 2025 snapshot, with the four core indicators Dalio uses to judge sustainability.

The line that matters is the first one, but the second is the one that bites. The United States carries the largest debt-over-revenue ratio in the group, 578%, at the lowest cost, 3.2%. Brazil carries a proportionally smaller debt, 430%, at the highest cost among the economies with their own currency, 14.25%. An eleven-percentage-point gap in carrying cost, with relatively larger debt on the American side, isn't explained by comparative fiscal discipline. It reflects the reserve-currency premium, expressed in operational terms. The world finances the US Treasury at a cost no other issuer gets, and that shows up directly when you place cost alongside the stock, not in the debt-over-GDP ranking.

Reading the stock alone understates how much this weighs on cash. Debt service consumes about 43% of all Brazilian government revenue, against 18% of US revenue. Brazil spends more than double the share of its revenue collection just to roll over interest, despite owing proportionally less. It's the same reserve-currency premium, now expressed in what's left over for the rest of the budget after paying the creditor. Argentina, on paper, spends only 7% of revenue on cash interest, but the figure is deceiving: most of the cost of its securities capitalizes into the stock itself rather than being paid, which artificially lowers the apparent debt service while the debt grows from within.

There's a maturity premium hidden inside the reserve-currency premium. Brazilian debt is mostly indexed to the Selic rate or short-term, so a high interest rate hits the stock almost immediately. American debt has long maturities and fixed coupons, and only absorbs a rate hike as bonds mature and roll over, about a third of the stock per year. The United States absorbs the tightening slowly, Brazil almost immediately, and Argentina, at the extreme, rolls over bills of just a few months, so that any interest-rate shock passes through to cost almost instantly. The same nominal rate weighs differently depending on the speed at which the debt reprices, and that speed is part of what Dalio observes when he analyzes maturity structure.

The reserve-currency premium is the variable that dissolves the paradox of the United States living with the highest leverage and the lowest short-term tension. It doesn't show up in the debt-over-GDP ranking. It shows up when you ask how much the debt costs, not how much it weighs.

What the 2025 Snapshot Doesn't Show

The reserve-currency premium isn't a permanent attribute. It's a variable, and the United States itself is eroding it. Dalio is direct about the mechanism: governments that hold a reserve currency tend to abuse the privilege, borrowing more than enough to lose it, which makes the decline sharper when it comes. Today's adverse gap isn't a passing anomaly. It coexists with primary deficits the Congressional Budget Office projects at US$ 2.9 trillion through 2034. The question isn't whether the privilege exists, but for how long the market keeps renewing it under current conditions. The premium buys time, but doesn't by itself resolve the solvency trajectory.

Argentina: The Metric Under the Exchange Rate

Argentina hides something different and more uncomfortable. In it, the metric rebels against the analyst, because the problem lies in the yardstick itself, not just in what it measures.

I redenominated the Argentine series in pesos, following Dalio's rule of measuring debt in the currency of denomination. The result revealed that Argentina's debt-over-revenue ratio isn't a single number. It's a range, and the width of that range depends entirely on which exchange rate is used to convert the debt.

On a dollar basis, converted at the year's average exchange rate, the ratio orbits around 400% throughout the period. On a peso basis, converted at the closing exchange rate, it explodes and comes to exceed 1,000% in 2023. The table below shows both series. The gap between them is brutal, and it isn't fiscal. The explanation is the December 2023 maxi-devaluation, which pushed the year-end debt to an exchange rate of 808 pesos per dollar while the year's GDP had been measured at an implicit average exchange rate of about 296. The jump is an artifact of the moment at which the exchange rate is snapshotted.

There's a sanity check that points to which basis is more consistent. Argentina's debt-over-GDP ratio on a peso basis, about 78% at the end of 2025, matches what official sources and market aggregators report for the country, while conversion at the average dollar exchange rate produces a lower figure, near 67%. To compare each country in its own currency, as is done with Brazil and the United States, the peso basis is the one that fits the standard. The dollar reading tends to understate, which is why I treat both bases side by side instead of picking whichever is more convenient.

The trajectory of the three geographies on the same scale makes the difference in nature evident. Brazil and the United States swing a few points a year. Argentina swings by hundreds, and the amplitude depends on which exchange rate is chosen.

This sheds light on an episode that, without the decomposition, would be misread. In 2024, Argentina carried out the largest fiscal adjustment of the trio, from a primary deficit of 2.9% of GDP to a surplus of 1.8%. And yet its debt-over-revenue ratio, measured in dollars, worsened from 390% to 470%. The cause wasn't spending. It was peso-denominated debt appreciating in dollar terms after exchange-rate stabilization, while dollar GDP shrank. Dalio would identify this as the mistake of measuring debt in the wrong currency. The adjustment happened. The indicator hid it.

I need to be explicit about a limit of my own construction, because it conditions how much can be claimed. For 2023 and 2024, I don't have Argentine revenue measured independently, and I assume it represented 16% of GDP, consistent with the only measured year, 2025, when it came in near 16%. Under that assumption, Argentina's debt-over-revenue ratio is just the debt-over-GDP ratio multiplied by a constant. This text's central innovation, measuring over revenue rather than GDP, gets neutralized precisely in Argentina's case. For Brazil and the United States, revenue is measured year by year and the distinction is informative. For Argentina, it adds nothing, and it's honest to say so before the sophisticated reader notices on their own.

With this choice of basis made, Argentina's stabilization gap is calculable, and in 2025 it was favorable. With nominal national accounts growth of about 45%, the rate that would stabilize the debt comes in near 47%, above the roughly 40% the debt effectively pays. The resulting gap is approximately negative seven points, and the observed data confirms the direction: debt over revenue on a peso basis fell from 526% to 489% over the year. If nominal growth had been the 34% of end-to-end inflation, the debt would have risen, and it fell instead, which rules out that reading.

The nature of this deleveraging matters more than its sign. It comes from inflation, not growth. Most of the 45% nominal growth is price repricing, not productive expansion, and inflation erodes the peso debt stock faster than interest rebuilds it. Dalio would call this inflationary deleveraging, not beautiful deleveraging. It's favorable and fragile at the same time, because it unravels if disinflation knocks down nominal growth or if a new exchange-rate jump reprices the dollar-linked share of the debt.

There's also the capitalization of the LECAPs, capitalizing bills, which added up to about 10 trillion pesos in 2024 and 2025 without passing through the cash result. It doesn't change the debt-over-revenue ratio, because it's already in the stock. But it contaminates the reading of the primary surplus. A formal primary surplus doesn't mean the debt is being paid down, when the central bank's remunerated cost is absorbed by interest that capitalizes into the stock itself. A green primary balance and growing debt can coexist, and in Argentina's case, they do.

Where the Math Doesn't Close

None of these readings is a clean snapshot, and acknowledging the limits is part of the rigor.

The Argentine dollar series is distorted by the exchange rate, and the peso series is distorted by a mismatch between the year-end stock and the revenue flow measured in average-value pesos, which are cheaper under 45% inflation. The two bases err in opposite directions, which is why I present both instead of pretending precision in one. The Brazilian projections beyond 2026 depend on four layers of assumption, spanning Focus, the budget, and the fiscal framework, and they stand as an order of magnitude, not as a precise point. Brazil's projected debt-over-revenue level, something like 491% in 2028, is a repetition of the official projection, not an independent derivation. What I hold with conviction in this projection is the gap, which follows from observable growth and primary balance, not the exact level of the stock. And the 2025 American stability is sensitive to less than one point of nominal growth, which already shifts it to slightly adverse.

There's also a scope limit, prior to the data. Dalio's framework isolates a specific mechanism, the dynamic between interest, growth, and primary balance over the debt stock. It doesn't measure productivity, demographics, institutional quality, reform capacity, or political stability, factors that also determine a country's solvency over the long run. An adverse stabilization gap signals pressure on the debt trajectory, not a destiny. What I'm comparing here is that mechanics, not the complete economic health of the three geographies.

I state these limitations not to weaken the argument, but because an argument that survives the disclosure of its premises is stronger than one that depends on hiding them.

What Dalio's Yardstick Reveals

Brazil, the United States, and Argentina face the same mechanism, with radically different intensities and instruments. The interest rate that stabilizes the debt is calculable for each of them. And none of the three is operating with room below it in the 2025 base scenario.

Brazil runs with a gap of more than four points, and the market consensus doesn't see the primary adjustment that would close it. The United States already runs with an adverse gap, of two to three points, shielded by a reserve-currency premium that it is itself eroding, with the budget curve pointing upward. Argentina had a favorable gap in 2025, the only one of the trio, but through inflationary deleveraging, not growth, and in a regime where the reading of debt still depends heavily on the exchange rate.

Dalio gives a name to what comes next, when the gap doesn't close. If the cost of debt rises because the market judges it unsustainable, the perception feeds on itself. Higher interest raises credit risk, which reduces demand for the bonds, which pushes the interest rate even higher. This is what Dalio calls the debt death spiral. The ways out are known, and all are costly: austerity, which contracts the economy because one person's spending is another's income; default or restructuring, which is deflationary because one person's debt is another's asset; central bank issuance, which is inflationary and devalues the currency; or tax increases. None of these ways out is painless, and the choice comes down to which cost to bear. It's worth noting that Brazil and the United States are cited in the book itself as cases where social spending has become too large to cut without political controversy.

The conclusion isn't about which country is worse off. It's about what this lens adds. When GDP is complemented with revenue, and the question becomes not just how much is owed, but at what price what is owed gets carried, the three cases stop looking like separate risk categories and become distinct points on the same equation. And that equation, unlike the debt-over-GDP ranking, allows projecting the path ahead, not just describing the present.

Sources

Ray Dalio, How Countries Go Broke, 2025, Chapter 3, pages 69 to 96.

Banco Central do Brasil, Boletim Focus of July 24, 2026. Ministério da Fazenda, Relatório de Avaliação de Receitas e Despesas for the first bimester of 2026. Ministério do Planejamento, 2027 budget guidelines bill (projeto de lei de diretrizes orçamentárias). IBGE, IPCA. Copom, decision of June 17, 2026, Selic at 14.25% per year. Banco Central do Brasil, net nominal interest accrued in 2025, about R$ 1.0 trillion, and international reserves, about US$ 360 billion in November 2025.

Congressional Research Service, IN12045, debt held by the public of US$ 30.277 trillion in fiscal year 2025.
