item.title: From Global Inflation to the Client's Portfolio: The Chain That Ran Through Expert XP 2026
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: The 16th edition of Expert XP took place between July 23 and 25 at São Paulo Expo, with 350 speakers, more than 120 hours of programming, and 64,000 attendees, according to the organizers. The edition marked…
item.content:encoded:
The 16th edition of Expert XP took place between July 23 and 25 at São Paulo Expo, with 350 speakers, more than 120 hours of programming, and 64,000 attendees, according to the organizers. The edition marked XP Inc.'s 25th anniversary.

Panels with Janet Yellen, Gabriel Galípolo, Niall Ferguson, and an anthropologist specializing in high-net-worth individuals occupied different rooms and addressed topics that do not overlap. Seen together, they cover distinct links in the same causal chain, one that connects the global supply shock to an allocation decision made by a client in the interior of Minas Gerais.

Supply shocks and artificial intelligence set the floor for the global cost of capital

Janet Yellen, former US Treasury Secretary, opened the first day with Caio Megale, XP's chief economist. She described an environment of successive supply shocks that keep US inflation above the 2% target over a five-year horizon. On rates, she said the Fed is in a holding pattern, but ready to raise rates if tension in the Middle East escalates.

The counterintuitive part came on artificial intelligence. According to Yellen, AI is currently raising inflation, not reducing it, because there is still no evidence of an aggregate productivity gain that would justify a change in monetary policy. The parallel she drew was with the late 1990s, when the Federal Reserve bet on productivity gains from the internet. The difference is that in that cycle the gain showed up in the data; in this one, it has not shown up yet, while investment in AI infrastructure is already pressuring demand for energy, equipment, and skilled labor.

On the dollar, Yellen acknowledged gradual erosion of its share in global reserves, from more than 70% to just above 50%, but maintained that there is no alternative market with the same depth, liquidity, and institutional backing.

Niall Ferguson closed the first day with Artur Wichmann, adding the geopolitical vector to the same mechanism. He framed the dispute between the United States and China as the defining relationship of the coming decades and pointed to the Taiwan Strait, not the Strait of Hormuz, as the world's most dangerous problem today, due to the concentration of global semiconductor production there. Fragmentation of the supply chain is a permanent supply shock, and a permanent supply shock is structural inflation, which means high rates.

In the CEO panel, moderated by Rafael Furlanetti, the same theme appeared from the real economy side. Gilberto Tomazoni, of JBS, explained the preference for acquisition over building from scratch based on prior knowledge of the asset. Paulo Moll described Rede D'Or using AI to capture information from medical records and support diagnosis. André Bier Gerdau Johannpeter addressed longevity as adaptive capacity and argued for separating the board from operations in succession planning. And Ederson Muffato gave the event's most unexpected piece of information by identifying online betting as the main competitor to food retail, since both compete for the same household income.

In Brazil, fiscal imbalance turned high rates into a prolonged condition

The second day moved down from the global scenario to the domestic mechanism, and the transition was direct: if the global cost of capital is high, the Brazilian cost of capital is even higher, and the reason is fiscal.

Gabriel de Barros, of ARX, estimated the need for structural adjustment starting in 2027 of around 4% of a GDP projected at R$ 13 trillion, something close to R$ 500 billion, with gross debt approaching 85% of GDP. Bruno Funchal, of Bradesco Asset and a former Treasury official, added the institutional point: a written fiscal rule does not produce credibility on its own; there must be a genuine willingness to spend below the ceiling for the effect to materialize. Dario Durigan, executive secretary of the Finance Ministry, presented the government's reading, attributing the year's inflationary pressure to the Iran war, rejecting the thesis of election-year fiscal expansion, and citing a primary adjustment equivalent to about 2% of GDP.

Gabriel Galípolo, in the monetary policy panel, addressed the consequences of this for the Selic rate and took the opportunity to respond to a recurring accusation with data, not rhetoric. The thesis that the Central Bank calibrates rates by listening only to the financial market, which would have an incentive to project high IPCA, is testable. Since the fourth quarter of 2023 the Central Bank has run the Firmus Survey, which asks non-financial sector companies about the same variables as the Focus Bulletin, created in 1999. If the accusation held, the productive sector's expectations would systematically come in lower than the market's. According to Galípolo, throughout the series they have come in equal to or higher than the market's.

What the two surveys show unambiguously is that de-anchoring is not a phenomenon restricted to the financial market. In the Firmus survey released in June 2026, with 349 companies surveyed in May, the median IPCA for 2026 rose from 4% to 5%. The Focus Bulletin from July 20 showed 5.15%. The two figures are not directly comparable, since they were collected two months apart and in that interval there was an escalation in the Middle East and an oil shock. But both point in the same direction, with the productive sector and the financial market projecting IPCA well above the 3% target.

Galípolo described the Central Bank as moving like an ocean liner, not a jet ski, defended restrictive rates for a longer period, and avoided signaling the next move on the Selic. Among the long-term pressure factors, he listed oil, El Niño, and investment in artificial intelligence. It's worth noting the convergence with Yellen the day before: two central banks, in different economies, treating AI as a short-term inflationary factor, not a disinflationary one. Convergence between monetary authorities is a shared reading, not proof. Both are observing the same channel, infrastructure investment pressuring demand for energy, equipment, and labor, and there is a counter-argument that cost deflation in technology-intensive services is already underway and would show up in the data with a lag. What both affirm is that this second leg has not yet appeared with enough magnitude to change the monetary policy decision.

High and prolonged rates change the definition of what protects wealth

This is where the chain reaches the portfolio, and this is where the event produced its most technical contribution.

Artur Wichmann and Ruy Ribeiro presented the study, also signed with Eduardo Marinho. The structural argument: the CDI offers predictability over a horizon of approximately 45 days, the interval between Copom meetings. For longer terms, the investor carries reinvestment risk and unanticipated inflation risk. During the inflationary shock of 2020 and 2021, the CDI's real return was negative, with the investor losing purchasing power while the statement showed a growing balance.

Ribeiro proposed the conceptual inversion: the risk-free asset is the one that protects against not reaching the goal, not the one that swings less tomorrow. And he showed that an NTN-B held for two years shows lower purchasing-power volatility than the CDI over the same period, which runs counter to the intuition of anyone looking at daily mark-to-market.

The inversion has a limit that needs to be made explicit, because the panel addressed horizon, not liquidity. The NTN-B protects purchasing power when held to maturity. An unplanned need to redeem along the way exposes the investor to mark-to-market, and the nominal loss in that scenario can be significant. The CDI carries reinvestment risk and inflation risk, and carries no nominal capital risk or liquidity risk. These are risks of different natures, not different degrees of the same risk. That's why the CDI remains the right instrument for an emergency fund, transactional cash, and any short-term or undetermined-term liability. The mistake the panel describes is not using the CDI; it's using it as a benchmark for long-term wealth protection.

The connection to the previous link is direct. The CDI's implicit promise for long terms is the stability of the rate that defines it. That rate is set by a monetary authority that, as the fiscal and monetary panels on the same day made clear, operates under fiscal constraints and works with scenarios of pause and resumption. Betting on long-term predictability of a very-short-term instrument is betting on a stability that the previous panels themselves classified as uncertain.

The day before, Rodrigo Sgavioli had already formulated the question this panel answered, observing that anyone investing in CDI doesn't know what the return will be in ten years.

Two private credit panels showed the other side of the same movement. Delano Macêdo, of Solis, addressed retail access to senior FIDC shares, made possible by CVM Resolution 175, in effect since October 2023, betting on a fund-of-funds structure instead of direct purchase. And Petrônio Cançado, of Occam, alongside Pierre Massari Jadoul, of ARX, and Leonardo Ono, of Legacy, raised the question of the sustainability of the tax exemption on incentivized debentures under Law 12,431, pointing to the practical problem of investors buying expecting traditional fixed-income behavior and instead finding long maturities, IPCA indexation, and mark-to-market volatility. It's the same CDI issue seen in the mirror: the right instrument, the wrong horizon in the mind of the buyer.

Thiago Maffra had established the commercial implication of this on the first day, in the panel on XP's 25th anniversary, by saying that the next frontier of advisory services is selling a solution, not a standalone product, incorporating tax planning, estate planning, and insurance into the scope.

The final link is behavioral, and it's where correct strategies tend to fail

A technically correct allocation to long real rates produces mark-to-market swings. This means the right strategy delivers, in the short term, a worse experience than the wrong strategy. The last link in the chain is what determines whether the client stays.

Michel Alcoforado, an anthropologist with fifteen years of research on high-net-worth individuals in Brazil, described the pattern of managing one's lifestyle always one notch above income, which increases debt and reduces investing capacity. He also noted that family wealth in Brazil typically lasts five generations, and that breaking that cycle depends on the family understanding that it needs to hand down to the next generation at least what it received.

Andre Agassi, in conversation with José Berenguer, described the turning point of 1997, when he fell to 141st in the ranking and then returned to the top: the difference was shifting focus to the next point instead of reacting to scoreboards. Rodrigo Nogueira, "Minotauro," in the retirement planning panel moderated by Luiza Valdetaro and Rodrigo Saldanha, addressed the distinction between achieving success and preserving it, and the need to turn to specialists after early-career mistakes.

At the event's close, João Fonseca, Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, and Caio Amato, Oakley's global president, addressed the same theme from the perspective of elite athletic performance. Fonseca described pressure as a privilege to be channeled and said he doesn't want to be the next Guga, but rather to build his own story.

The complete chain

Global supply shock and geopolitical fragmentation sustain structural inflation. Structural inflation sustains high rates. In Brazil, fiscal imbalance prolongs high rates beyond what activity would justify. High and prolonged rates change the operational definition of what counts as a safe asset, shifting the axis from nominal floating-rate instruments to long-term real rates. And long-term real-rate assets swing, which transfers the problem from the technical field to the behavioral one.

No single panel at Expert XP 2026 contained this entire chain. Each one contained a link, with its own data and its own expert. For those who work with asset allocation, the event's value wasn't in any specific panel — it was in seeing the links fit together.

Sources

Panels from Expert XP 2026, São Paulo Expo, July 23 to 25, 2026, with coverage from InfoMoney, Poder360, O Tempo, Forbes Brasil, NeoFeed, Times Brasil/CNBC, Bora Investir/B3, Seu Dinheiro, BPMoney, Bem Paraná, and Cointelegraph Brasil.

Paper "Repensando o ativo sem risco: uma visão brasileira," Artur Wichmann, Eduardo Marinho, and Ruy Ribeiro (XP, Atlantiqis, and Insper, 2026).

Pesquisa Firmus and Boletim Focus, Banco Central do Brasil. Resolução CVM 175. Lei 12.431/2011.

Attendance, speaker, and plenary audience figures released by the event's organizers. The fiscal adjustment estimate is a projection by ARX Investimentos. The assessment of the betting market's size is a statement from the Grupo Muffato executive.

Note: InfoMoney belongs to the XP Inc. group.

item.title: The Discount Rate Governed the First Half of 2026
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: One principle explains the American rally, the Brazilian correction, the long bond massacre, and Bitcoin's decline.
item.content:encoded:
One principle explains the American rally, the Brazilian correction, the long bond massacre, and Bitcoin's decline.

By the cultural yardstick of the Brazilian investor, a good half-year is one in which the stock market rises. In the first half of 2026, the stock market rose. The Ibovespa advanced 6.76%, the S&P 500 hit new highs, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index doubled in value.

The CDI yielded 6.90% over the same period.

With the CDI at this level, the ranking flips. Whoever held the Ibovespa saw the index rise 23% through mid-April, give back 13% by the end of June, and finish behind those who accepted no volatility at all. The premium for taking equity risk in Brazil was, in realized terms, negative. And this was not a local accident. It was the Brazilian manifestation of a principle that governed the entire half-year, across every geography and every asset class.

The Half-Year Rewarded Present Cash and Punished Promise

The principle is simple. When the real interest rate is high, the discount rate becomes the dominant factor in price formation. Every year of waiting costs dearly, and the present value of a distant cash flow shrinks more than that of a near one. The practical consequence: assets that deliver cash now beat assets that promise cash later, unless the promise grows fast enough to offset the larger discount. That exception decides the top of the ranking.

The mechanism explains the hierarchy of returns, and its top is reached by two distinct paths. One is the mechanical carry of high interest rates: CDI-indexed debentures yielded 7.09% and the Tesouro Selic, 6.95%, simply by capturing the Selic rate at the level it was at. The other is the exception of the promise that comes true: semiconductors led the half-year, driven by memory makers, not because they have short duration, but because earnings revisions, anchored in results already delivered, ran faster than the rise in the cost of capital. Their high multiple embeds future growth, like every high multiple, but it was growth that earnings releases kept confirming quarter after quarter. They beat the gravity of the discount through the numerator, not by escaping it. In the middle, the conditional promise: the Ibovespa, which depended on falling rates to unlock its discount and got neither a sufficient cut nor an earnings shock, delivered 6.76% with pain. At the bottom, pure promise: the longest Brazilian government bond lost about 15% in June alone, and Bitcoin, which promises no cash flow at any date whatsoever, fell 33%.

The pattern is not new. The year 2022 in the United States ran the same movie, with rates rising, unprofitable tech melting down, and energy paying off. The difference in 2026 is that Brazil lived both ends at once: a rally bought from abroad and a discount rate that never stopped charging its toll at home.

The Brazilian Stock Market Rose in Two Acts and Lost on the Final Scoreboard

The first act lasted until April 14. Driven by the largest foreign capital inflow for a start of the year since 2022, with R$ 26.3 billion in January alone, the Ibovespa climbed from 161,125 points at the end of 2025 to a closing record of 198,657 points, a gain of 23.3% in a little over three months. The accumulated foreign net flow for the year neared R$ 67.7 billion by mid-April, and foreign investors accounted for 61% of B3's trading volume.

The second act began right there. Between the record and the end of June, the index gave back 13.4%, with an 8.24% decline concentrated in the second quarter. Foreign investors withdrew R$ 14.9 billion in May and another R$ 8.8 billion in June, and the half-year net flow in the secondary market closed at R$ 33.8 billion. The flow that manufactured the rally also manufactured the correction.

Meanwhile, short fixed income was doing the quiet work. The CDI accumulated 6.90%, and only two ANBIMA indices beat that mark: CDI-indexed debentures, at 7.09%, and the Tesouro Selic, at 6.95%. At the long end, the massacre. The IMA-B 5+, which tracks the longest inflation-linked bonds, yielded 2.20%, less than a third of the CDI, with the ten-year real rate nearing IPCA plus 7.5% and the Tesouro IPCA+ 2035 paying as much as 8.10% in real terms in June.

The American Rally Had Earnings. The Brazilian Rally Had Flow

Here lies the half-year's central argument, and it requires looking at both markets at once.

In the United States, the S&P 500 rose 10.2% backed by earnings. Consensus expected 13.1% growth for first-quarter results; the actual figure came in near 28%, with 84% of companies beating estimates, and the 2026 earnings growth projection was revised from 13.6% at the start of the year to 23.3% by the end of June. An honest caveat: part of the surprise came from non-operating accounting items at three tech giants, and broad-based growth, excluding these effects, came in near 14%. Even so, the direction is unambiguous. Analysts spent the half-year revising American earnings upward.

In Brazil, the movement was the opposite. Cumulative revisions to the Ibovespa's projected 2026 earnings added up to an 11.5% decline through April, with expected full-level growth cut to 5.8%, dragged down by commodities and by the real's appreciation. The Brazilian rally of the first quarter did not buy expanding earnings. It bought a discount, and a qualification is in order here. The index traded at 9 to 10 times earnings, below the historical average of 10.5, but this aggregate multiple is skewed downward by the weight of Vale and Petrobras at a commodity cycle peak, which inflates the denominator's earnings. Excluding the two, the multiple rises to the 11-to-12 times range, at or above the historical average. The apparent price was flattened by top-of-cycle commodity accounting. The real price, with the distortion removed, was no bargain. By this very text's yardstick, it was worse: paying 11 to 12 times earnings with the ten-year real rate at IPCA plus 7.5% narrows the equity premium over real fixed income to a thin band. It was not a discount, it was a thin premium. The rally did not buy cheap fundamentals. It bought the bet, financed by foreign flow, that falling rates would restore the premium that high rates had compressed.

Fact and inference need to be kept separate at this point. The fact is the asymmetry of revisions: American earnings up, Brazilian earnings down. The inference is mine: the B3 correction was less a judgment on Brazil and more the local effect of a global risk repricing, triggered when earnings showed up on one side of the map and not the other. The domestic deterioration in inflation and rates helped, but the trigger was external.

It's worth not tracing where that capital went, because the data do not support any clean destination. It did not go back to the United States: during the half-year, equity flow left there, with non-US equity ETFs accounting for 34% of inflows, against a market share of 20%. Nor did it migrate to Asian tech emerging markets, the most intuitive hypothesis after the strong performance of Korea and Taiwan in the first months of the year: in June, these two markets were the epicenter of the emerging-market equity sell-off, not its destination, with US$30.5 billion pulled out of South Korea, the largest foreign outflow in more than 25 years, and US$18.3 billion from Taiwan. It wasn't rotation from one market to another. It was the same factor compressing everything at once. The IIF attributed the June outflow to higher global discount rates and sensitivity to positioning in technology. It is this text's yardstick on a global scale: when the discount rises, the long promise loses in any time zone.

The engine of this American earnings story has a name and address: the physical supply chain of artificial intelligence, and within it, memory. Nine of the twelve largest contributors to the S&P 500 during the half-year were chip and memory companies, and Micron alone accounted for 16% of the index's gain, with a 304% rise over the period. SanDisk rose 858%, the largest gain in the entire S&P 500. Nvidia, already repriced in the prior cycle, rose 7%, and the Magnificent Seven fell 2%: leadership did not come from the GPU maker, but from memory suppliers, where earnings surprised this half-year. The market is no longer paying for the promise of AI. It is paying for the earnings of those who sell its infrastructure, and distrusting those who must turn the US$725 billion in annual capex from the four largest platforms into revenue. For now, every dollar invested in infrastructure generates about ten cents of AI revenue. The picks-and-shovels thesis won the half-year precisely because downstream monetization remains unproven.

Data center euphoria reached Brazil as an even longer-dated promise. The up to R$ 200 billion announced in the country promises cash further out than American capex, and without the present-tense earnings that carried semiconductors: the country operates less than 1 gigawatt, connection requests total 26 to 38 gigawatts, nearly 80% of curtailed power occurs precisely in the Northeast of these projects, and the sector's tax regime lapsed in February and awaits the Senate. If the market distrusted even American capex, which is at least backed by current revenue, the Brazilian bet is a decade-long one, not a 2026 catalyst. The same discount that rewarded memory's present earnings punishes any promise that distant.

Bitcoin Spent Six Months Refuting the Thesis That Made It Famous

If the half-year punished promise, Bitcoin was the most exposed promise of all.

The asset fell 33% in dollar terms, from US$87,700 to US$58,600, and closed June more than 50% below its October 2025 high. Ethereum lost 47%. US spot ETFs recorded their largest monthly outflows since launch. And Strategy, the market's largest leveraged Bitcoin vehicle, saw its multiple over net asset value fall below 1, made its first coin sale since 2022, and announced a program authorizing the monetization of up to US$1.25 billion in BTC. With the multiple below 1, every new share issued destroys Bitcoin per share instead of creating it, and Strategy's leveraged accumulation model reverses. What broke was the vehicle's engineering, not the asset's protocol, which keeps issuing at its same old algorithmic pace. Bitcoin's price fell on its own, under the weight of interest rates, not dragged down by Strategy.

The reading matters more than the numbers. The dominant thesis of the previous cycle was that of an uncorrelated store of value, digital gold. A half-year with war in the Middle East, oil above US$126, and pressured global inflation was the ideal scenario for that thesis to work. It didn't work. Bitcoin fell alongside long bonds and against the grain of AI stocks, behaving like the market's longest-duration asset, a cash flow promised for never. What this half-year failed was the uncorrelated store-of-value function, in the perfect scenario for it. The scarcity thesis and the network-adoption thesis were not at stake here: they are decided over years, not six months. A bad quarter brings down a hedge, it doesn't judge a protocol.

A narrative is circulating that capital migrated from crypto to AI stocks. I record it as a hypothesis, not as fact. The simultaneity is real, but calendar correlation doesn't prove flow. The more parsimonious explanation is a common factor, the liquidity squeeze from high real rates, which punishes the cashless speculative asset and rewards the asset with proven earnings.

The Local Investor Did the Exact Opposite of the Foreigner

This is the data point that retrospectives ignore, and it's the half-year's most revealing one.

Month by month, Brazilian institutional investors operated as a mirror image of foreign capital. While foreigners bought R$ 26.3 billion in January, locals sold R$ 17.5 billion. February, March, and April repeated the pattern. In May and June, when foreigners withdrew R$ 23.7 billion, locals bought back R$ 16.7 billion. Accumulated through the end of June: foreigners plus R$ 32.9 billion, local institutions minus R$ 33.0 billion. Locals sold the entire rally and bought the entire correction.

In realized terms, institutions got it right: they sold in the 185,000-to-190,000-point range, with selling concentrated near the April peak, and bought back near 172,000. But analytical honesty demands the caveat. Part of this selling wasn't conviction, it was cash to pay redemptions. Local equity funds lost R$ 11 billion in net inflows for the year, while international equity funds raised R$ 11.8 billion. Brazilian fund investors swapped the local stock market for the foreign one, the same risk at a different address, a move that high carry does not explain. Less allocation calculus, more fatigue with the market itself.

And the destination of domestic capital tells the rest of the story. Secondary-market turnover of incentivized debentures reached R$ 179.4 billion between January and May, a record for the period in the historical series, up 32.7% over 2025. The detail almost no one read: primary issuance fell 5.8% over the same span. This isn't the market financing more infrastructure. It's the same stock of tax-exempt paper churning faster and faster among investors competing for carry. Brazilian capital did not migrate toward risk. It migrated toward yield, and yield paid off.

The Half-Year This Text Describes Has Already Ended Differently

Every thesis needs boundaries, and this one has three.

The first is geopolitical. The half-year closed under a Middle East truce that pushed Brent down from US$126 to US$73. That truce collapsed on July 8, and the barrel returned to the US$85-to-90 range. America's June inflation relief, with the consumer price index falling 0.4% for the month, its largest monthly drop since 2020, is a child of cheap oil. The connection to the thesis is direct: cheap oil loosens inflation, lower inflation opens room for the Fed, and the Fed's room defines the global discount rate that ordered every price this half-year. A shock that reignites oil runs this chain in reverse and re-tightens the discount across every market at once.

The second is commercial. On July 16, the United States announced an additional 25% tariff on Brazilian goods, effective July 22. The exclusions for coffee, beef, orange juice, and aircraft reveal a design meant to minimize American domestic inflation. The direct economic impact on Brazil is sectoral and manageable, and that's not how it enters the thesis. A US tariff on Brazil does not move the global discount rate. It moves the local risk premium, through a political channel: in an election year, the tariff becomes fuel for the fight, and the fight is the largest generator of idiosyncratic risk premium on the Brazilian curve in the second half. It is through this domestic discount, not the global one, that it reaches prices.

The third bounds the central thesis itself. The argument that the Brazilian discount has no catalyst depends on inflation staying pressured. The most recent data point in the opposite direction: June's IPCA rose 0.16%, half the projected median of 0.31%, and the twelve-month accumulated figure slowed from 4.72% to 4.64%, while Focus still projects 5.30% for December. The yield curve prices in a deterioration that, for now, is not materializing. If the next readings confirm disinflation, the Copom, which cut Selic to 14.25% in June, gains room, the real rate gives way, and the stock market's discount finds exactly the trigger that was missing in the first half. Add the October election, historically the largest generator of idiosyncratic volatility on the Brazilian calendar, and the second half is far from a simple extrapolation of the first.

The Yardstick Decides the Verdict Before the Return

The first half of 2026 was not a contest between stocks and fixed income. It was a demonstration that, with real rates at this level, the discount rate governs every price. It chose the winners in the United States, manufactured and dismantled the Brazilian rally, crushed long bonds, and stripped Bitcoin bare.

The question of the yardstick remains. Saying the stock market lost to the CDI is true, and that's what this text did. But choosing the CDI as a universal benchmark is itself an analytical decision, not a law of nature. The paper Repensando o ativo sem risco, by Marinho, Ribeiro, and Wichmann, published in June, argues that the risk-free asset is a function of each investor's liabilities, and that for long horizons the inflation-linked bond fills that role better than the floating-rate one. By the CDI yardstick, whoever held long inflation-linked bonds lost badly during the half-year. By the yardstick of a long-term real liability, whoever held them locked in IPCA plus 7.5% for a decade, and may have made the best trade of the six months.

Return is a number. The verdict depends on the yardstick. And the yardstick, in Brazil, is almost never discussed. It's inherited.

Sources: B3 (Ibovespa closing levels and investor flow, December 30, 2025 to June 30, 2026); ANBIMA (CDI, IMA and IDA indices, 1H2026; Incentivized Debentures Bulletin, January-May 2026); IBGE (June 2026 IPCA, release dated July 10, 2026; Quarterly National Accounts, 1Q2026); Central Bank of Brazil (Copom, 279th meeting, June 17, 2026; Focus); BLS (June 2026 CPI, release dated July 14, 2026); EIA and CNN Business (Brent: 1Q26 close at US$118 and intraday high of US$126.41 on April 30, 2026); FactSet Earnings Insight and Charles Schwab (S&P 500 earnings, 1Q2026 and 2026 consensus); RBC Wealth Management (1H2026 equity retrospective, July 1, 2026, FactSet/Bloomberg data: Philadelphia Semiconductor Index return, Micron and SanDisk returns, Micron's contribution to the S&P 500 gain); Institute of International Finance, IIF (June 2026 Capital Flows Tracker, via Reuters, July 10, 2026: outflows from South Korea and Taiwan); State Street Investment Management and Bloomberg (equity ETF flows, 1H2026); XP Investimentos, Raio-XP via InfoMoney and Exame (Ibovespa earnings revisions and monthly flow, data through June 26, 2026); Elos Ayta and Quantum Finance (foreign flow; balances vary depending on the universe considered: R$33.8 billion in the secondary market excluding public offerings, R$36.7 billion including offerings); CoinDesk and market data (Bitcoin and Ethereum in dollars; spot ETFs); Marinho, Ribeiro, and Wichmann, Repensando o ativo sem risco, June 2026; FT and corporate earnings releases for 1Q2026 results (aggregate capex of US$725 billion from the four largest hyperscalers in 2026, versus US$410 billion in 2025). Methodological note: flow figures cited in the body use the June 26 Raio-XP data for the monthly foreign-versus-institutional comparison and the June 30 closing figures for the half-year balance.

item.title: From the Spreadsheet with Solver to AI Orchestration: A Process Account on Dividend Portfolio Optimization
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: This does not constitute investment advice or securities analysis. The author is not a CVM-accredited analyst. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
item.content:encoded:
This does not constitute investment advice or securities analysis. The author is not a CVM-accredited analyst. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

The spreadsheet with Solver solves the portfolio optimization problem. It maximizes the Sharpe ratio, respects relative constraints on the weights, and converges to a solution in seconds. The problem is what it does not allow with rigor and scale at the same time: separation between the calibration period and the test period, a dynamic risk-free rate retrieved via API, a static backtest with six years of history, and auditable methodological boundaries. Not because it is impossible in Excel, but because the implementation cost is high enough that simplification beats rigor most of the time.

What changes when AI enters as the implementation environment, and what does not change, is what this text describes.

AI did not replace analytical judgment. It tore down the implementation barrier.

The design process was deliberately dialogical, not hierarchical. Each architectural choice came after at least one round of exchange: I proposed a direction, Claude or Gemini brought up implications I had not mapped out, and the adjustment followed from there. Separating calibration from testing into fixed windows, retrieving the CDI via the Central Bank API instead of using a fixed rate, setting the bounds at 50% to 200% over the analyst's weights, redistributing the weights of discontinued tickers among the remaining ones instead of discarding the portfolios: each of these decisions went through this dynamic. The weight redistribution, for example, came along with the observation that tickers with no data tend to be discontinued or problematic, which constitutes a mild form of survivorship risk. Knowing this before finalizing the decision is exactly what the dialogical process adds. Responsibility for the choices is mine. The path to reaching them was shared.

The code, the script structure, and the iterative execution of each version were Claude's.

There is a mistaken version of how to use AI in analytical work: throw the problem at the tool and accept the output. What works is different. AI is the implementation environment. The analyst is the architect of the decisions. When this hierarchy is inverted, the result is code that runs but answers poorly formulated questions.

What the Experiment Showed

The test used two recommended dividend portfolios from two Brazilian firms, exactly as published in June 2022, with tickers and weights verified against the original PDFs. The optimizer, a Sharpe maximizer with constraints relative to the analyst's weights, was calibrated exclusively with data from June 2019 to May 2022 and tested from June 2022 to June 2026. As a passive benchmark, DIVO11 was used, a dividend ETF with history over the full period. The CDI over the test period, drawn from BCB series 11, was 13.1% per year.

The result was asymmetric between the two firms.

In the first portfolio, the optimizer delivered an annual return of 25.3%, an excess of 12.2 percentage points over the CDI, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.65. The analyst delivered a 19.7% return, 6.6 points of excess, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.39. In the second portfolio, the result reversed: the analyst delivered a 17.3% return, 4.2 points of excess, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.22. The optimized portfolio delivered a 14.4% return, 1.3 points of excess, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.08, practically identical to the passive DIVO11, which delivered a 14.3% return and the same 0.08 Sharpe ratio over the period.

The explanation for the reversal is the mechanism that Michaud formalized in 1989: the optimizer concentrated two-thirds of the second portfolio in three assets based on what was optimal within the calibration window. In the test period, what was optimal in-sample did not hold up out-of-sample. And the detail that matters is in the decomposition: the concentrated portfolio had lower volatility than the analyst's (16.7% versus 18.9% per year). The cost of concentration was not taking on more risk. It was betting on expected returns for the wrong assets. The analyst's more uniform distribution proved more defensible precisely against this estimation error in returns, which is the core of Michaud's argument, and not against an excess of volatility that did not occur.

An earlier experiment in the series quantified this same mechanism via bootstrap: with 500 random splits and training windows of about 80 trading sessions, the optimizer's median Sharpe ratio ranged from 1.9 to 3.0 in-sample and fell to 0.16 to 0.59 out-of-sample, an average degradation of 88%. In a later round with three-year calibration windows, the degradation disappeared. Estimation error is not a binary defect in the model: it is a function of the size of the window that feeds it.

The asymmetric result invalidates any categorical claim in either direction: the optimizer does not always beat the analyst, and the analyst is not always more defensible than the model.

Adversarial Instruction Detects. Analytical Domain Expertise Validates, Prioritizes, and Corrects.

This separation was not clear before running the experiment. The initial hypothesis was that formulating the right question for the reviewer was the hard part, and that whoever did not know what look-ahead bias was would not be able to ask the reviewer to look for it. What happened was different.

The instruction given to Gemini was generic: act as a rational reviewer, identify logical inconsistencies, point out design biases, without making concessions in tone. Look-ahead bias was detected under this instruction, without my naming it in advance. The error was concrete: the first version of the experiment used the portfolios' current composition applied retroactively, as if the 2022 analysts had recommended on that date what they recommend today. Gemini pointed out that any result generated by this design would be invalid, because the optimizer would be calibrated with information that did not exist at the time of the allocation decision. The correction required going back to the firms' original PDFs and rebuilding the portfolios with the exact tickers and weights from June 2022. The same holds for the criticism of causal attribution in the conclusion, which the reviewer identified without specific instruction about this type of flaw. In both episodes, the adversarial instruction was enough for the reviewer to find the problem. Analytical domain expertise came in afterward: to understand the criticism, assess whether it was valid, and correct it precisely.

Gemini was not the only review layer. Grok and ChatGPT came in for targeted cross-checks, when a second source reduced the risk of confirmation bias between the reviewer and the model that implemented the experiment. Claude in implementation, Gemini in continuous adversarial review, the others in sample-based verification: it is this division of roles, with asymmetric and explicit instructions, that the title calls orchestration.

The most defensible thesis, then, is not that the bottleneck lies in the quality of the questions you ask the model. The bottleneck lies in two distinct phases. Adversarial instruction opens the space for error detection. Analytical domain expertise closes the space for correction. Without the first, errors tend not to surface through the reviewer. Without the second, errors surface but are not corrected, or are corrected in the wrong direction.

A caveat about the models' default behavior: the advantage of the AI reviewer over the human reviewer exists, but it is conditional on adversarial instruction. The default behavior of LLMs is to endorse what was presented, not to challenge it. Explicit adversarial instruction is what turns this default into useful criticism. Without it, the AI reviewer reproduces the same problem as a human reviewer with no autonomy to disagree.

When This Process Does Not Work

The process described has limits worth naming before replicating it.

Analytical domain expertise is a prerequisite for the correction phase, not for detection. Someone without that expertise can obtain the adversarial criticism, but cannot assess whether it is valid or apply the correct fix. The reviewer points out the problem, and the analyst does not know whether or how to correct it. The validation ecosystem is only as effective as the expertise of whoever operates it at the correction stage.

The experiment also operates with a small sample: two portfolios, one realization of the test period. It is not statistically generalizable. It is evidence of direction, not proof of a rule. A rigorous test would require multiple firms, multiple periods, and significance tests on the estimated Sharpe ratios. The standard error of a Sharpe ratio calculated over four years of data is wide enough to make most results formally inconclusive from a statistical standpoint.

The experiment carries two regime caveats that come as a pair. The test period (CDI at 13.1% per year) was structurally different from the earlier low-rate cycle, which raises the bar for any variable-risk portfolio and systematically compresses the Sharpe ratios. The calibration window (June 2019 to May 2022) contains the March 2020 crash, which makes the optimized weights strongly dependent on that period's regime. If one regime caveat applies, so does the other.

The Bottleneck Is No Longer the Tool.

And it is not just the quality of the questions.

It is the combination of adversarial instruction with analytical domain expertise: the first opens the space for error detection; the second ensures that the errors found are corrected in the right direction. Removing either one reduces the system to one of its halves, and neither half works on its own.

The code runs in minutes. The experiment with look-ahead bias runs just as fast and produces equally convincing numbers. The difference is not in execution speed. It is in having the validation process that finds the error before publication, and the expertise to know what to do when it appears.

Resources and Tools

The complete Python scripts for the experiment, including data collection via Yahoo Finance and BCB, a static IS/OOS backtest with maximum-Sharpe optimization, and historical Monte Carlo simulation, are available in the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alissondpoliveira/mvo-carteiras-dividendos-b3

A simplified Excel version, where the user enters the tickers and weights of their portfolio and receives return, volatility, and Sharpe ratio with a dynamic CDI, is available for download: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1OVdUqc2cqz6GwP23iWI_XMNPzwv0PWsX/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=114003155137833182047&rtpof=true&sd=true

item.title: ETFs in Brazil in 2025: Real Growth, Still Indeterminable Causes
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: In December 2025, 919,000 individual investors held ETF positions in Brazil — almost double the figure from two years earlier. The asset class's assets went from R$54 billion to more than R$91 billion over the…
item.content:encoded:
In December 2025, 919,000 individual investors held ETF positions in Brazil — almost double the figure from two years earlier. The asset class's total assets went from R$54 billion to more than R$91 billion over the year. Fixed income ETFs, which until 2024 occupied a marginal share of the sector, became the center of gravity for inflows.

There are two explanations with a real mechanism behind this growth. The problem is that both occurred within the same 12-to-18-month window — and public data does not separate the weight of each.

This article does not pick a winner. It explains why doing so is not possible with the available data, and describes what would be needed to resolve the question.

What Grew, When, and Who Bought

The jump in assets mixes two things that need to be separated: new money and mark-to-market appreciation. In a year of high Selic rates, part of the increase is appreciation of assets already in the portfolio, not inflow. That is why the gross figure is not the most important metric. The relevant metric is the change in investor composition — and that change is unambiguous.

In January 2025, individual and institutional investors split ETF holdings in close-to-even proportions — about R$19 billion for individuals versus R$34 billion for institutions, in total assets of R$58 billion. Over the course of the year, individual investor holdings grew 49%. By December, individuals accounted for between 78% and 81% of the ETF industry's total assets. Fixed income ETFs specifically closed the year with 721,700 investors and R$26.9 billion in custody — a figure with no public breakdown by investor type.

The year closed with net inflows of R$13 billion, according to B3's Annual ETF Report — a reversal of two straight years of net redemptions. That figure is net inflow: subscriptions minus redemptions, excluding market appreciation. The R$37 billion in total asset growth (from R$54B to R$91B) combines that net flow with the appreciation of assets in the portfolio. The change in composition that accompanies this flow is verifiable and is not explained by mark-to-market: institutional investors did not disappear from the portfolio; they were diluted by retail growth.

The product shelf also expanded: 62 new ETFs were listed on B3 over the course of the year — versus 16 in 2024 and 13 in 2023 — broadening access to strategies previously restricted to large allocators.

This rules out the reading that the driver was institutional. Retail was the vector of the compositional change. But it does not say — yet — why.

Four Explanations, Two Ruled Out

There are four candidate explanations. Two fail the timing test. Two survive.

One candidate explanation is supply: more products, simpler platforms, lower minimum tickets. It fails because the first fixed income ETF listed in Brazil, IMAB11, has existed since May 2019. Supply was available for five years without meaningful traction. If supply were the cause, growth would have started in 2019. It is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

Another candidate is "investor maturation" — a recurring claim in market reports. It fails because it has neither a mechanism nor a date: it describes the result and labels it a cause. "The investor became more mature" explains ETF growth the same way "the teams scored more goals" explains a final score. It is true and it is useless.

Two remain.

Distribution friction. The dominant channel in the Brazilian market is the investment advisor (assessor de investimentos), compensated through commissions and rebates on the products they distribute. ETFs pay low or zero rebates. Where this compensation logic prevails, there is a structural incentive not to offer ETFs to the client — not out of bad faith, but by design of the model. The market today operates under three basic configurations: the commission-paid advisor, still predominant; the advisor operating under a fee-based model tied to a financial institution; and the securities consultant (consultor de valores mobiliários) registered with CVM, who works for a fixed fee and can serve clients at any institution. CVM Resolutions 178 and 179, in effect between November 2024 and January 2025, imposed transparency on compensation and demarcated these models more precisely. Over the same period, the base of consultants registered with CVM grew 28%. The decline in friction, in this reading, comes from the advance of fee-based models in their various forms — the institutionally tied advisor who began charging for the service, or the independent consultant — and from the migration to the self-sufficient investor, who dispenses with any intermediary.

Product merit under high interest rates. Fixed income ETFs deliver a measurable tax advantage over traditional fixed income: no come-cotas, no IOF, with exchange liquidity and low cost. In traditional funds, the tax authority withholds tax twice a year, reducing the capital working for the investor. In an ETF, tax is only due upon sale. The compounded advantage, calculated under the regime in effect after MP 1,303 lapsed in October 2025, reaches 0.92 percentage points over two years, 2.8 points over five, and 6.2 points over ten. With the Selic at an elevated level in 2024 and 2025, this advantage applied on top of a high nominal return, making it even more legible in the investor's net account.

The Problem That Prevents Picking a Winner

Here is the knot. The Selic rose and the channel changed in the same window: 2024 to 2025. In statistics, this has a name — collinearity. In market practice, the problem is simpler to state: when two forces push the same car at the same time, you cannot look at the speed and pin down which of the two pushed harder.

Consider the investor who put money into a Tesouro Selic ETF at the end of 2025. Did they do it because high interest rates made the tax exemption irresistible on paper? Or did they do it because, for the first time, they reached a channel — a fee-based consultant, or simply the home broker — that had no financial incentive to hide that product from them?

The question has no answer in open data. With the Selic high and the channel shift occurring at the same time, any observed ETF growth is compatible with product merit, with the decline in commercial friction, or with both in a proportion that public series simply do not isolate. Claiming that "it was the channel shift" or "it was the tax merit" based on these series is not analysis — it is narrative choice dressed up as conclusion.

Declaring this indeterminacy is not weakness. Exposing that the market is buying a manufactured certainty is the real advantage of the analysis.

What the International Evidence Says — and Does Not Say

The literature on the effect of the distribution model on asset allocation is consistent in direction.

Christoffersen, Evans, and Musto (2013), in the Journal of Finance, showed with data from U.S. funds between 1993 and 2009 that payments to brokers are associated with greater inflows into funds with worse future performance. The conflict of interest in the commission-based model produces adverse selection for the investor.

When the United Kingdom banned commissions to advisors in 2013 (Retail Distribution Review), Morningstar analysts directly linked the ban to the migration toward passive funds. The Netherlands achieved a similar result: a decline in product costs beyond the eliminated commission, with a shift toward passive management above the average of other European countries.

Sebastian, Noth, and Grafe (University of Regensburg, 2023), in a panel of 38 OECD countries between 1997 and 2020, estimated a difference in wealth returns of 1.5% to 2% per year between countries with and without a commission ban — with an estimated cumulative loss for Europe of €375 billion per year. The study drew strong criticism from the financial industry, which should be noted by anyone citing it.

The limit of the analogy is precise: the United Kingdom and the Netherlands imposed the ban through state coercion, forcing immediate migration. Brazil operates in a free market, with competition between the commission-based and fee-based models. CVM Resolutions 178 and 179 did not ban commissions — they imposed transparency. The international literature proves that the direction of the effect exists. It does not prove that the Brazilian transition will have the speed of the ban cases, nor that it is inevitable.

What the Self-Sufficient Investor Changes in the Equation

There is a point that the channel narrative does not directly resolve.

The individual who bought an ETF in 2025 could have arrived through three paths: a fee-based consultant, a commission-paid advisor (structurally improbable, but not impossible), or a self-sufficient investor — opening the home broker, reading about come-cotas, buying alone, with no intermediary at all.

There is no public cross-reference between ETF inflows and the originating channel. B3 and ANBIMA publish ETF growth. CVM publishes consultant growth. No one cross-references the two databases.

If the flow is predominantly self-sufficient, the narrative of the "fee-based revolution" loses the prominence attributed to it. The product simply sold itself on its own merit, without needing a new type of advisor to reach the investor. This does not mean channel friction is irrelevant — the investor who chose the home broker also dispensed with the commission-paid advisor, which is itself a form of reduced friction. But it dissolves the specific claim that fee-based consultants were the central vector of growth.

In this reading, the channel explanation and the product-merit explanation not only converge: they become nearly indistinguishable. A good product in a frictionless channel is, at the same time, a product that won on merit and a channel that stopped blocking it. Calling them separate causes becomes a distinction without available empirical support.

What Would Settle the Question

Waiting for the Selic to fall does not solve the problem. A drop in interest rates does not switch off the product's merit — it merely trades the appeal of a high nominal return for the appeal of relatively low cost, since an active fund's fee weighs more heavily when the CDI shrinks. An ETF withstanding a rate cut is compatible with product merit the entire time. The time-based test is inconclusive by construction.

The valid isolation is by comparing groups, not by time. At a given moment, with the same Selic, the same tax regime, and the same products available, ETF merit is identical for all investors. If merit is the driver, adoption should be similar between clients of commission-paid advisors and clients of fee-based consultants. If channel friction is the driver, adoption diverges: high in the rebate-free channel, low in the commission-paid one.

Two data sets would make this test possible. The first: ETF adoption by distribution channel, controlled for investor profile — this would isolate the effect of the conflict of interest between professionals. The second: a breakdown of ETF purchase flow by order origin, advised account versus self-directed account, within the same platforms — this would measure how much of the phenomenon goes through any intermediary at all.

Neither data set is available in public sources. The market today tracks the phenomenon through aggregated databases, without cross-referencing flow origin by channel. Until these databases converge publicly, attributing ETF growth to a single cause — whether the advisory model or the tax merit — will remain in the realm of speculation.

What the available metrics allow us to state without ambiguity is that the structural shift in allocation is real. The jump to 919,000 investors and the R$13 billion in net inflows prove that retail has definitively adopted the vehicle. Whether through the legibility of the tax gain, the natural decline in commercial friction, or — what is mathematically more likely — the indivisible combination of both forces in the same time window, the ETF has stopped being a secondary-shelf product and become the portfolio's center of gravity.

This article is for analytical and academic purposes only. It does not constitute investment recommendation, financial advice, or any form of counsel. The author is not a credentialed securities analyst. The analyses presented here are retrospective, based on public data, and should not be used as a basis for investment decisions.
