item.title: Election Polling and Prediction Markets: The Category Error in Market Comparisons
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: It has become routine in political and financial circles to directly compare traditional election polls with numbers coming from prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. Since the…
item.content:encoded:
It has become routine in political and financial circles to directly compare traditional election polls with numbers coming from prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. Since the 2024 American election cycle, analysts have pitted these data points against each other with every new release, frequently pointing out that markets priced in a Donald Trump victory while opinion aggregators showed a statistically tied race. This attempt to overlay the two indicators is constant, but it starts from a flawed analytical premise.

The core problem with these recurring comparisons is not determining which tool has greater predictive power. It lies in a fundamental methodological confusion: the two instruments are not measuring the same object.

Treating polls and prediction markets as direct competitors ignores the microstructure of each tool. A poll is not a prediction market without financial incentive, and a market is not a poll without controlled sampling. They have distinct measurement objects, distinct operational mechanisms, and they deliver outputs that belong to completely different mathematical categories.

What election polling measures

Election polling is a classic exercise in statistical inference about a continuous variable. The method is based on selecting a sample that replicates the demographic makeup of the voting population, recording declared responses, and then extrapolating to the entire electorate using weighting techniques.

The resulting data point — "candidate A has 44% voting intention" — represents an estimate of vote share subject to a specific margin of error and confidence level. It is not a probability of victory, but a snapshot of expected electoral density if the election were held on the date the data was collected.

The vulnerabilities in this process are methodological and sample-based in nature. Non-response bias occurs when certain voter profiles refuse to participate or conceal their true preference due to social stigma, as observed in the systematic underestimation of support for Trump in 2016 and 2020 in specific districts of the American Rust Belt. Sampling error arises when the "likely voter" model does not match the electorate that actually turns out to vote. These factors distort the raw data before any analytical interpretation even takes place.

The question that polling sets out to answer is strictly descriptive: if the election were held today, how would votes be distributed across the population?

What prediction markets measure

On a prediction platform, agents trade contracts tied to a binary outcome: the candidate wins or does not win. The equilibrium price reached in the order book reflects the implied probability the market assigns to the event. If a candidate's contract is quoted at $0.60, the market is signaling a 60% probability of victory — not that he will win 60% of the vote.

The mechanism is grounded in the aggregation of dispersed beliefs through a competitive pricing system, a theoretical line that traces back to Friedrich Hayek's arguments on market efficiency and was popularized by James Surowiecki in The Wisdom of Crowds (2004). The underlying assumption is that agents operating with capital at risk (skin in the game) process fragmented information with greater speed and efficiency.

Unlike the pollster, who extracts the voter's declared choice, the market requires the bettor to price who will come out the winner, financially punishing wrong calls. The absence of demographic representativeness in the order book does not invalidate the instrument; a commodities trader does not need to be a farmer to correctly price a corn futures contract. The market operates as a price discovery mechanism, not a population census.

In The Myth of the Rational Voter (2007), Bryan Caplan shows that the absence of a direct individual cost to political voting allows systematic cognitive and ideological biases to proliferate. Since any single vote rarely changes the outcome, holding irrational beliefs generates no economic penalty for the individual. In prediction markets, the dynamic runs in reverse: bias or analytical error is costly. The financial incentive acts as a selection force, penalizing traders guided by dogma and rewarding factual accuracy.

However, the efficiency of this mechanism is not absolute. A Vanderbilt University study (Clinton & Huang, 2025) analyzed Polymarket's behavior during the 2024 cycle and found that 58% of presidential markets showed negative serial correlation in the final weeks. This translates into sharp price swings and reversals over very short periods — a classic symptom of noise trading. The concentrated demographic profile of these platforms (predominantly young, tech-investor, and liberal-libertarian leaning) introduces a wishful-thinking component that the financial incentive reduces but does not eliminate.

The question answered by the market is forward-looking: given the information available, what is the statistical probability of each outcome materializing?

The category error

The most common analytical error in market comparisons is equating voting intention with probability of victory. They do not express the same mathematical quantity.

Brazil's political scenario in May 2026 exposes this distortion. The Datafolha poll shows Lula leading the first round with 38%, closely followed by Flávio Bolsonaro with 35% — a gap of just 3 percentage points, constituting a statistical tie at the edge of the margin of error. At the same time, Polymarket and Kalshi quotes price final victory probabilities at 45% (or 46%) for Lula and 33% for Flávio. The gap between the frontrunners jumps to 12 percentage points in the betting environment, where the poll shows tight proximity. Both data points coexist validly, since they measure different dimensions of the same phenomenon.

The divergence becomes even more evident when looking at lower-profile candidates, such as Renan Santos, who registers 2% voting intention in the descriptive poll but reaches between 8% and 10% implied probability in prediction markets. Strictly speaking, we do not know the exact source of this gap of up to 8 percentage points, and the isolated design of these tools does not allow us to trace its causal origin. An overly generous reading would suggest the market is anticipating complex long-tail scenarios that escape statistical sampling. However, applying Occam's Razor, the most probable explanation, aligned with the Vanderbilt evidence, is demographic: Renan Santos (co-founder of MBL) has strong digital penetration precisely within the demographic niche that trades crypto assets and frequents these platforms. The 10% on Polymarket likely reflects wishful-thinking bias and the low liquidity of the Brazilian order book, not a qualified predictive read of invisible street-level trends.

Methodological criticism of prediction markets should focus on their structural flaws, not on the absence of sampling. The first major risk is capital concentration. When a handful of accounts dominate a contract's financial volume, the principle of opinion diversity that underpins the wisdom of crowds is broken. In the 2024 election, a single French trader concentrated roughly $80 million in positions favoring Trump on Polymarket, controlling up to 20% of the shares on one side of the book. Although he was anchored to his own modeling strategy (neighbor polling) that proved profitable, the episode exposed how vulnerable prices are to the actions of large whales.

The second constraint lies in the microstructure of contracts outside the central geopolitical axis. On Kalshi, which operates under CFTC regulation and attracts institutional capital from prop trading desks, compliance rules tend to mitigate egregious manipulation. However, this instrument's track record in political races is still short and lacks robust empirical validation. For the Brazilian market in May 2026, where liquidity is thin, Kalshi's prices (46% vs. 33%) track Polymarket's (45% vs. 33%) closely through pure algorithmic arbitrage via API. Treating them as two independent validation indicators is an analytical illusion: bots are simply mirroring the signal from one platform onto the other.

The loop that contaminates both

The two instruments do not function as isolated laboratory variables; they operate under a regime of causal feedback.

The market is an information derivative. Its main primary input is the polls themselves. When a significant new poll is published, the order book reacts instantly, adjusting quotes. If the polling ecosystem is operating under a hidden statistical bias, the market will absorb and propagate that initial error, as happened with the chain reproduction of sampling flaws that preceded the 2016 American election.

The reverse vector also holds true. The economic literature documents the bandwagon effect, in which segments of fickle or undecided voters tend to align their vote with the candidate who publicly presents as the apparent frontrunner. Subsequent opinion polls end up capturing this alignment movement, turning the market's price expectation into real voting intention on the ground.

In a recent paper, Nechepurenko (2026) formalizes this behavior through the lens of conditional reflexivity. In high-exposure environments, the implied probability published by these platforms stops being a mere mathematical projection and starts acting as a focal point for political coordination. It guides the tactical behavior of campaign donors, sets the tone of news coverage, and steers political parties in forming coalitions and choosing running mates. The price signal does not merely predict the future; it alters agents' incentives and helps build it.

A sketch of a model

Since the instruments measure distinct variables and are subject to different types of error, the correct approach for the analyst is neither to discard one in favor of the other nor to run a simplistic weighted average between voting-intention rates and victory probabilities.

The mathematically consistent path involves a Bayesian Updating process. The election poll should be treated as the prior — the starting probability distribution, grounded in rigid, descriptive demographic data. The prediction market enters as the information-updating vector, continuously pricing the risk that the prior is wrong. The market absorbs so-called tail risks: legal volatility, the possibility of disqualifications, last-minute scandals, or extraordinary political developments that traditional questionnaires cannot map in real time.

Research conducted by UCLA Anderson (Chernov, Elenev & Song, 2024) shows that structured combination of these estimators reduces the variance of final forecasts, provided the sources of error are not fully correlated. And this is where the practical limit lies for the analyst in the Brazilian context: in low-liquidity, shallow-depth markets like Brazil's in 2026, signal independence collapses. If the trader prices the contract by consulting the same Datafolha poll that the financial market reads, and if Kalshi's bots arbitrage their prices based on Polymarket, the Bayesian model loses operational traction. Instead of an update rich in independent data, the combination can result in a tautological loop that merely adds psychological noise on top of the initial statistical estimate.

Conclusion

Directly overlaying election polling with prediction markets constitutes a mathematical category error.

The poll estimates voting intention: a continuous variable, drawn from descriptive sampling, designed to answer how many votes each candidate commands at the present moment. The market prices probability: a binary outcome, synthesized through financial orders, designed to answer who has the best conditions to win given the tree of possible scenarios and all the associated uncertainty.

Confusing vote share with implied probability of victory means ignoring the nature of the numbers. The poll describes the ground on which the race unfolds; the market calculates the odds of crossing the finish line under different weather and track conditions. They do not cancel each other out, do not replace each other, and should not be mixed linearly. The analytical gain lies in understanding the microstructure of each signal to map where street-level sampling ends and where future-risk pricing begins.

References

Clinton, J. & Huang, T. (2025). Are Betting Markets Better than Polling in Predicting Political Elections? arXiv:2507.08921.

Nechepurenko, M. (2026). Price as Focal Point: Prediction Markets, Conditional Reflexivity, and the Politics of Common Knowledge. arXiv:2604.24147.

Chernov, M., Elenev, V. & Song, D. (2024). The Comovement of Voter Preferences. UCLA Anderson Review.

Graefe, A. (2018). Polls to Probabilities: Comparing Prediction Markets and Opinion Polls. International Journal of Forecasting.

Caplan, B. (2007). The Myth of the Rational Voter: Why Democracies Choose Bad Policies. Princeton University Press.

Datafolha (May 12–14, 2026). Presidential poll — first-round voting intentions. n=2,004, margin ±2pp.

Kalshi (May 2026). Brazil Presidential Election — KXBRPRES-26. kalshi.com/markets/kxbrpres/brazil-presidency/kxbrpres-26.

Polymarket (May 2026). Brazil Presidential Election (winner). Volume: $77.5M. polymarket.com/event/brazil-presidential-election.

item.title: The Facade Renovation: Why Brazil in 2026 Looks Beautiful, But Is Short-Circuiting.
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: The house looks impeccable. Trimmed garden. Fresh paint. Lights on in every room. The engineer who read the electrical blueprint knows what's behind the walls.
item.content:encoded:
The house looks impeccable. Trimmed garden. Fresh paint. Lights on in every room. The engineer who read the electrical blueprint knows what's behind the walls.

Brazil in 2026 presents a set of indicators that, read in isolation, look like a snapshot of a healthy economy. Read together — within a debt cycle model — they reveal the portrait of a peak disguised as a launch pad.

The Most Seductive Facade of All Cycles

Before the diagnosis, a necessary acknowledgment: this cycle's facade is exceptionally well built.

The average real wage of workers rose. Employment advanced. Household consumption climbed. These aren't fabricated figures — they're real movements of an economy that, in the short term, delivered a tangible improvement in living standards for a significant share of the population.

The problem isn't the facade's existence. The problem is the material it was built with.

When real income rises without an equivalent productivity gain, it has two possible sources: redistribution (someone pays the bill) or debt (the future pays the bill). In Brazil in 2026, both sources operate simultaneously. The state redistributes via deficit spending. Households complete consumption via credit. Labor productivity grew just 0.4% in 2025 [FGV IBRE, 2026] — far from justifying, on a self-sustaining basis, the real income increase observed.

Income gains without productivity gains aren't prosperity. They're the anticipation of future consumption, paid with interest.

The Glow of the Dead Star

When you see a star in the sky, you're seeing a past event. The light left thousands of years ago. The star may no longer exist.

Unemployment works the same way: it records the accumulated outcome of a cycle that has already happened. It doesn't anticipate the next one.

The PNAD Contínua recorded an unemployment rate of 5.1% in the quarter ended December 2025 — the lowest level in the historical series that began in 2012 [IBGE, 12/2025]. By March 2026, the rate had already risen to 6.1% [IBGE, PNAD Contínua, 04/2026].

The historical low in unemployment isn't the start of a new era. It's the precise technical signal that the expansion consumed all available idle labor. When there's no more slack to absorb, the cycle has nowhere left to grow along that path. The lagging indicator photographs the past — and the past has already turned.

Fresh Paint and Melting Wiring

GDP grew. Consumption advanced. The facade is new.

Behind it, the accumulated nominal deficit over the twelve months through March 2026 reached R$ 1,217.5 billion — 9.41% of GDP [BCB, Fiscal Statistics, 04/2026]. That's the real hole in public accounts, with the full cost of debt included. The primary result — the metric the government displays — excludes interest and communicates management where there is liability accumulation.

The generator keeping the lights on is called Selic, set at 14.5% per year by the Copom on April 29, 2026 [BCB, 04/2026]. This rate applies to Gross Debt of R$ 10.1 trillion — 78.7% of GDP [BCB, 01/2026]. The fuel bill exceeds R$ 1.2 trillion per year. For every R$ 100 the economy produces, nearly R$ 10 go toward servicing what the government owes.

The dynamic is a snowball: high debt generates high interest, high interest increases debt. The fresh paint is on the walls. The wiring is melting inside.

Malinvestment and Crowding-Out: When the Generator Hijacks Savings

In the technical vocabulary of capital theory, this has a name: malinvestment.

When artificial credit and deficit spending replace market price signals, resources flow not to where real productivity points, but to where the stimulus points. The result looks like growth. It's capital misallocation that only holds up as long as the generator keeps running.

There's an additional mechanism that criticism of the deficit frequently omits: crowding-out. Selic at 14.5% per year with a real rate of approximately 9.5% turns Brazilian government bonds into the lowest-risk, highest-return asset available in the domestic market. Capital that could finance innovation, capacity expansion, and productivity gains in companies migrates, rationally, toward financing government debt. The State doesn't just spend poorly — it hijacks the available savings that would finance private productive investment.

Productivity data confirm the diagnosis. In 2025, labor efficiency grew just 0.4% in the aggregate [FGV IBRE, 2026]. Services fell 0.6%. Industry dropped 0.3%. The only sector with real gains was agribusiness: +13.2% — precisely the sector that finances its expansion with its own capital and access to global markets, without depending on the domestic credit hijacked by the state generator.

More people working to produce proportionally the same output. The engine is running in neutral. The fuel is being burned by the generator, not by the growth engine.

Households' Overdraft

The consumption sustaining growth was bought on credit.

In March 2026, 80.4% of Brazilian households had some form of debt — the highest percentage in the entire historical series of the PEIC, conducted by CNC since 2010 [CNC/PEIC, 03/2026]. 29.6% are past due. The average delinquency period reached 65.1 months — more than five years of open installments [CNC/PEIC, 03/2026]. Serasa tallied 81.7 million delinquent borrowers in February 2026, after 14 consecutive months of increases [Serasa, 02/2026].

When the borrower can no longer service the debt, they either stop consuming or stop paying. In both cases, the expansion cycle comes to an end. Brazil is at that inflection point.

Brazil, Japan, and Argentina: The Nuance Superficial Comparison Ignores

Two arguments circulate to downplay the fiscal diagnosis. One invokes Japan. The other suggests that debt in local currency and held by domestic holders protects Brazil from acute crises. Both have partial merit. Both are insufficient.

The domestic debt argument is correct — as far as it goes. Brazilian public debt is predominantly denominated in reais and financed by domestic creditors. This avoids the kind of abrupt external collapse Argentina has repeatedly faced, when the mismatch between dollar-denominated debt and falling reserves accelerated systemic crises. Brazil is not Argentina. That point deserves to be conceded.

The problem lies in the conclusion drawn from it. Domestic debt in local currency isn't cost-free debt — it's debt whose cost is paid by the economy itself, via potential inflation, via crowding-out of private investment, via compression of fiscal space for future countercyclical policies. Protection against an acute external crisis is not protection against slow structural deterioration.

The Japan argument fails on the number that matters. Japan finances debt of 250% of GDP with structurally elevated domestic savings at a real cost close to zero. Brazil's real interest rate stands around 9.5% per year — among the highest on the planet — applied to R$ 10.1 trillion of gross debt. In Japan, the generator runs on nearly free, internally generated energy. In Brazil, it burns imported diesel at a 9.5% annual real cost, on a stock that grows by mathematical inertia.

The difference isn't one of degree. It's one of nature. Two generators with radically different fuels.

The External Factor: The Wind That Can Delay, Not Change the Physics

A favorable external scenario — rising commodities, a weak dollar, falling international interest rates — can prolong the cycle longer than internal imbalances suggest. This is technically true and deserves to be said.

But a favorable tailwind doesn't change the physics of the wiring melting behind the walls. It keeps the star shining longer. It doesn't change what's happening inside it.

A favorable external scenario, when present, has one precise effect: it raises the cost of the future adjustment, because it allows internal imbalances to deepen longer before becoming unbearable. Every additional quarter of a 9.41%-of-GDP nominal deficit financed at a 14.5% Selic rate is one more quarter of snowballing. A favorable tailwind may make that quarter more comfortable. It doesn't make it neutral.

The Rally vs. The House Blueprint

Conclusion

This cycle's facade is the most seductive in decades. Real income rising, unemployment at a historical low, consumption heated up. The easy criticism is to ignore these figures. The rigorous criticism is to understand where they come from.

They come from a nominal deficit of 9.41% of GDP. From R$ 1.2 trillion in annual interest that hijacks the savings that would finance real investment. From 80% of households at the ceiling of indebtedness. From productivity that only grows where the State hasn't reached.

Domestic debt in local currency avoids Argentina. A 9.5% real rate on R$ 10 trillion prevents Japan. Brazil occupies a space of its own: able to avoid an abrupt external collapse, but unable to escape slow structural deterioration as long as the generator keeps running at this cost.

A favorable external tailwind can keep the star shining for another quarter or two. It doesn't change what's happening inside it.

"The question that remains isn't about the glow we see today, but about the integrity of the source. The market celebrates the facade. The prudent investor analyzes the wiring."

References

Technical analysis for educational purposes. Does not constitute investment recommendation.

item.title: Cetipados Funds in Brazil (2023–2026): An Analysis of Infrastructure and Allocation Dynamics
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: An analysis of the forces that generated 4,604 new vehicles in three years — and what the professional allocator needs to verify before allocating
item.content:encoded:
An analysis of the forces that generated 4,604 new vehicles in three years — and what the professional allocator needs to verify before allocating

Technical definition and starting point

A cetipado fund is not an investment category — it is a trading infrastructure category. The term distinguishes closed-end funds whose quotas are registered and traded on B3's organized OTC market (formerly CETIP), as opposed to exchange-listed funds, whose quotas trade in continuous trading sessions with price formation on screen.

This distinction has direct analytical consequences. In an exchange-listed fund, the quota price reflects market consensus at every trade: there is a bid, there is an ask, there is observable volatility. In a cetipado fund, the quota is calculated by the administrator based on the yield curve and the marking of the underlying assets — not on recent secondary market transactions. In the absence of continuous trading, the NAV reported to the quotaholder is an accounting estimate, not a market price. This has two implications that run through this entire text: the first is behavioral (the quotaholder sees no swings on the statement because there is no continuous price formation); the second is about risk (the absence of an observable price does not mean the absence of credit or market risk — it means that risk is deferred until the next forced pricing event).

With that technical foundation established: between January 2023 and April 2026, the number of new closed-end fund classes registered with CVM grew from 330 to more than 2,200 per year. What explains this growth, what it represents in terms of real risk for the quotaholder, and how a professional allocator should filter this universe are the three questions this text examines.

The mechanism that generated the boom

Every financial innovation cycle begins with a real problem and ends with product excess. The cetipados cycle began with two simultaneous problems, both real, both verifiable in the data.

The first problem was on the demand side. On January 2, 2023, the mandatory mark-to-market requirement for private fixed-income securities took effect in client portfolios of institutions bound by ANBIMA's Distribution Code: debentures, CRIs and CRAs began to be reported at updated market value, no longer at curve value. That same week, Americanas disclosed the accounting inconsistencies that triggered its judicial reorganization. According to an Itaú BBA estimate reported by Bloomberg Línea in March 2023, all funds with at least 15% of the portfolio allocated to private credit — a universe that includes multimarket funds, fixed-income funds and credit funds of every category — accumulated R$ 66 billion in net redemptions between January 12 and March 2 of that year. In the specific category of funds classified as private credit, ANBIMA recorded R$ 5.1 billion in redemptions in January and R$ 12.2 billion in February — R$ 17.3 billion for the period. The difference between the two figures reflects the scope of the universes measured: the R$ 66 billion impact captures credit exposure distributed across all fund categories, not only those nominally classified as such.

The combined effect was direct: the investor who had never seen volatility on the statement began to see swings of 2%, 3%, 5% in products considered conservative. Demand for instruments that would not display such variation became concrete. The closed-end fund solves this directly: the quota does not mark to market at the frequency the investor checks it, and the fixed term creates the perception of a controlled horizon.

The second problem was on the supply side. CVM Resolution 160, which governs public offerings of closed-end fund quotas, and CVM Resolution 175, in force since October 2023, standardized class registration and reduced the operating cost of creating and distributing cetipados. The regulatory infrastructure to launch these funds at scale came into existence precisely when behavioral demand existed to absorb them.

Two simultaneous problems, one solution in the same regulatory format. Understanding this overlap is what allows the growth to be assessed beyond the product narrative.

What the CVM data reveals

Between January 2023 and April 2026, 4,604 new closed-end fund classes were registered in the FII, FIP, FIDC and FIAGRO categories — the cetipável universe — in the registro_classe.csv and registro_fundo.csv datasets made available by CVM as open data. A methodological note is necessary: registro_classe.csv counts classes and subclasses, not unique CNPJs. RCVM 175 introduced the umbrella fund structure, in which a single CNPJ can concentrate multiple classes with distinct strategies and target audiences. A portion of the growth recorded in 2024 and 2025 reflects the reorganization of existing structures into new classes to comply with the new regulatory framework, in addition to the creation of genuinely new vehicles. CVM's open data does not allow this difference to be isolated directly, so the number of new CNPJs is lower than the number of registered classes. Real growth is significant under any counting methodology. The year-by-year evolution is direct:

2023: 330 new closed-end classes. 2024: 1,877, up 469% from the prior year. 2025: 2,299, an additional increase of 22%. 2026 (January to April): 98.

The acceleration from 330 to more than 2,200 new classes per year between 2023 and 2025 does not find proportional explanation in verifiable demand variation. The Selic rate went from 13.75% per year at the start of 2023 through a cycle that brought it to 10.5% by mid-2024, before a new upward move (BCB, COPOM history). High interest rates encourage the search for post-fixed credit instruments with a premium over CDI — which explains the direction of growth, but not the scale. The data point that would establish this relationship rigorously — the evolution of the average number of quotaholders per fund or average NAV per class over the years — is not available in CVM's open data in a format that allows direct isolation. What the data does allow us to state is that the growth in the number of vehicles has no equivalent correlate in aggregate fundraising per vehicle: total FIDC fundraising reached R$ 81.4 billion in 2024 (ANBIMA), while the number of new FIDCs grew 578% between 2023 and 2024 — suggesting fragmentation of the asset base across multiple vehicles, not proportional expansion of the investor base. The regulatory window, distribution incentives and the reorganization effect of existing structures under RCVM 175 account for a relevant part of the delta.

The composition by fund type reveals a relevant rotation. In 2024, FIDCs accounted for 1,218 of the 1,877 new closed-end funds, 65% of the flow, and the category's fundraising reached R$ 81.4 billion for the year, up 86.1% from 2023, according to ANBIMA. In 2025, FIDCs fell to 246 new classes, while FIPs rose to 1,157 and FIIs to 789: FIPs and FIIs went from 26% to 85% of the new classes registered in the year. This rotation coincides with the moment when net spreads on cetipado FIDCs proved lower than qualified investor expectations, and the flow of new registrations migrated toward structures with longer return horizons and less comparability with short-term benchmarks.

Administrative concentration confirms the supply-side logic. CVM's open data reveals that the largest administrator in the cetipado universe during the period figures in more than 640 of the 4,604 vehicles, 14% of the universe, with combined net assets exceeding R$ 240 billion. The three largest administrators combined account for more than 60% of total NAV. This degree of concentration reflects the scale advantage of consolidated platforms, which reduce the marginal cost of launching new vehicles. The data is derived from matching by administrator CNPJ in CVM's open data, excluding funds with NAV above R$ 50 billion.

The four forces sustaining the growth

The cetipados boom does not have one cause. It has four, operating on distinct layers with independent logics.

The first is behavioral, on the demand side. The mandatory mark-to-market requirement in effect since January 2023 and the Americanas episode created aversion to visible volatility. Not to real risk, but to the representation of risk on the statement. The closed-end fund solves this: the quota does not swing at the frequency the investor checks it, and illiquidity is framed as a feature, not a constraint. For high-net-worth investor profiles with long-term allocation horizons, this framing makes genuine sense.

The second force is regulatory and economic, on the supply side. RCVM 160 and RCVM 175 reduced the cost and time to create and distribute closed-end funds by standardizing class registration and public offering documents. From the supply side, the closed-end fund has a distribution compensation structure different from the open-end fund: the distribution fee is recognized when fundraising closes, whereas in the open-end fund the equivalent compensation tends to be diluted over the product's life cycle. This structural difference is a fact the quotaholder should incorporate when understanding the product being acquired.

The third force is structural and operates in corporate credit. With the Selic rate held above 10% per year since 2021 (BCB, COPOM history), mid-sized companies began seeking alternatives to bank credit. The FIDC allows receivables to be securitized directly in the capital markets, potentially at a lower cost than intermediated bank credit, without depending on a bank's balance sheet. The growth of aggregate FIDC NAV, which reached R$ 741.1 billion in the twelve months ended November 2025, up 22.5% in the period, according to ANBIMA data from December 2025, reflects this real demand for credit intermediation outside the banking system. The problem is not the instrument. It is that the same wrapper serves both to securitize receivables of a company with solid cash flow and to structure lower-quality assets with the appearance of structured credit.

The fourth force is fiscal, with a mechanism more specific than the usual formulation suggests. Law 14,754, enacted in December 2023, instituted semiannual withholding tax (come-cotas) on conventional closed-end investment funds — closed-end Multimarket Funds and Fixed Income Funds — eliminating the tax deferral these vehicles provided. The most direct impact was not on the retail investor acquiring FII quotas over the counter. It was on the wealth manager who structured closed-end exclusive and super-exclusive funds as accumulation vehicles with tax deferral for high-net-worth clients: these funds accumulated returns without periodic come-cotas; after the law, that deferral ended. Cetipado FIIs, Fiagros and FIPs became structural substitutes — they preserve the come-cotas exemption for individuals, which was never withdrawn from them. This is the more precise migration mechanism: not new investor demand for cetipados, but a reorganization of wealth governance structures toward vehicles with tax treatment equivalent to the previous one. The same law taxed offshore funds at a 15% rate starting in 2025. The claim that "repatriated offshore capital migrated to domestic cetipados" is plausible as a hypothesis; it is not documented in flow data available for this text and should be read as inference, not established fact.

What a representative sample reveals about the asset class

To the investor arriving at the segment by name alone, the cetipado universe appears homogeneous: closed-end funds, fixed term, no redemption window. Analysis of a sample of 43 active funds with confirmed distribution, covering FIIs, Fiagros, infrastructure funds and private credit structures, reveals the opposite. It is not one asset class. It is a spectrum ranging from senior secured credit with explicit subordination to pure equity with no return floor.

The spectrum of benchmarks

A cetipado fund's benchmark signals the nature of the risk assumed and the return horizon of the strategy. In the sample analyzed, four benchmark families coexist within the same regulatory universe — and the same fund category can operate with different benchmarks depending on the manager's strategy and the profile of the underlying assets.

The first family is CDI with a fixed spread. The spread observed in the sample ranges from 1.5 to 4.5 percentage points per year, with the floor associated with structures with greater protection — high subordination or solid real guarantees — and the ceiling present in strategies with greater relative risk, such as credit concentration or assets without external ratings. A relevant point for the individual investor: a significant portion of the cetipado universe is exempt from individual income tax on returns, which significantly raises net return relative to taxed instruments with an equivalent benchmark.

The second family is IPCA with a fixed spread. The range observed runs from IPCA + 4% to IPCA + 8%, with the ceiling concentrated in structures with greater perceived regulatory or execution risk. This benchmark implies long duration — the investor maintains exposure to the inflation index for the fund's entire term. The individual income tax exemption, where applicable, significantly amplifies net return in this format.

The third family is the fixed rate. A fixed return is viable in structures where the average turnover period of underlying assets is much shorter than the fund's term, allowing the manager to adjust portfolio yield without accumulating duration risk relevant to the quotaholder.

The fourth family is not a fixed-income benchmark: it is an IRR target. Funds that invest in project or company equity declare a target internal rate of return in their regulations, typically between 15% and 25% per year in nominal terms. This is the only format where the investor assumes pure equity risk — no return floor, no priority in the waterfall, no guarantee of principal return.

Risk architecture: waterfall, subordination and guarantees

The second dimension of diversity is the capital protection structure. Within the same regulatory universe coexist funds with multiple layers of protection and funds where the quotaholder is entirely exposed to the portfolio's residual risk.

In FIDCs, the most common structure is the division between senior and subordinated quotas. The senior has priority in cash distribution and principal return; the subordinated absorbs losses first, functioning as a protective cushion. The subordination ratio — the proportion of NAV held in subordinated quotas — is the main indicator of effective protection. Funds with 20% subordination offer radically different protection from funds with 5%, even if they share the same benchmark and stated term. More elaborate structures add a mezzanine tranche between the two extremes, creating a three-tier loss-absorption waterfall.

In cetipado receivables FIIs, protection comes from a different mechanism: a real guarantee on the properties backing the CRIs in the portfolio. The relevant question here is not about subordination, but about LTV — the ratio between the outstanding balance of the receivables and the updated value of the property given as collateral. A fund with an average LTV of 55% carries a significantly different protection cushion from a fund with an LTV of 85%, even if both present themselves as real estate receivables funds with a target return of IPCA + 6%.

In agricultural credit Fiagros, guarantees vary among crop pledges, fiduciary liens on rural property, producer guarantees and fiduciary assignment of export receivables. The quality and liquidity of these guarantees vary significantly by crop, by region and by commodity price cycle. Credit backed by exported soybeans has a different execution profile than credit backed by sugarcane crops destined for the domestic market.

In FIPs, there is no structural guarantee: the quotaholder buys stakes in companies or projects, and the return depends entirely on asset performance. Protection, where it exists, comes from contractual exit-preference clauses or ratchet mechanisms, not from subordination or real collateral. It is the format with the greatest information asymmetry between manager and quotaholder.

The sectors where capital is allocated

The third dimension of diversity is the destination of the capital. Mapping the sample by allocation sector, five blocks emerge with distinct characteristics of risk, cycle and underlying asset liquidity.

Logistics and corporate real estate: cetipado FIIs that acquire properties directly or finance their construction and acquisition via CRI. Return is composed of rental yield (entry cap rate) and capital gain upon sale at the end of the term. The main risk is vacancy and the real estate cycle. Asset liquidity is sufficient for guarantee execution within reasonable timeframes, which distinguishes this segment from others with less fungible collateral.

Agricultural credit: Fiagros that finance rural producers via CRA or directly structured operations. Return is directly linked to the commodity cycle, sector delinquency and the effectiveness of safeguards during periods of stress. The exceptional returns observed in 2025 in part of this sample reflect asset repricing following a delinquency cycle in 2024, not structural acceleration in profitability, and should not be extrapolated as a current return expectation for the segment.

Infrastructure: FIP-IE and FI-Infra funds that invest in debentures of solar and wind energy projects, transmission, basic sanitation and road concessions. Return is indexed to IPCA with a fixed spread and structured in predictable flows under concession contracts, provided the project does not face regulatory or execution risk. This segment concentrates the sample's longest duration and the greatest sensitivity to sharp moves in the real yield curve.

Corporate credit: FIDCs that acquire receivables from mid-sized companies, trade invoices and working capital operations. Risk is credit concentrated in the originator and in the quality of the receivables portfolio. The subordination structure is the main protection mechanism, and its effectiveness depends on the subordination ratio, portfolio diversification and the quality of the manager's origination policy.

Individual credit: payroll-deduction FIDCs, vehicle financing and unsecured personal credit. Risk is spread across thousands of individual debtors, which reduces specific concentration but exposes the fund to macroeconomic employment and income cycles systemically. Delinquency recovery rates vary significantly by modality: public-sector payroll credit has recovery close to 100% due to the payroll-deduction mechanism; unsecured personal credit, much lower.

What the diversity implies

Two cetipado funds with the same five-year term, the same classification as a limited-liability closed-end fund and the same classification on the distribution platform can have radically different risk profiles: a senior payroll-deduction FIDC with 20% subordination and an equity FIP in agro-industrial projects. The regulatory wrapper is identical. The content has no dimension in common.

This heterogeneity is not a flaw in the segment. It is its defining characteristic. And it is the strongest argument against any evaluation based on category: the product's name does not inform the product's risk.

Universe segmentation and structural risk map

The number 4,604 needs to be dissected before any inference. Treating it as a homogeneous mass is the first analytical error.

Two distinct groups make up this universe, with entirely different logics and risks.

Shelf products: vehicles designed for platform distribution, with public offerings and fundraising directed at the high-net-worth retail segment and qualified investors. It is in this group that oversupply risk resides — proliferation of vehicles without proportional growth in the investor base, and without manager selection keeping pace with the rate of launches. The growth from 330 to more than 2,200 new classes per year is, to a large extent, the story of this group.

Governance vehicles: structures created by Single-Family Offices, Private Banks and wealth managers to consolidate capital and optimize taxation following Law 14,754/2023. Family-participation FIPs, single-property FIIs, FIDCs holding receivables of the same economic group. These are not distribution products — they are infrastructural efficiency migrations. The same wealth, repackaged in cetipado format for tax or operational reasons. The risk here is not inadequate distribution. It is governance and intra-group asset pricing. Those who migrated for tax reasons know the vehicle they are using. Those who arrived through the shelf product generally know only the statement.

CVM's open data confirms this divide: dozens of funds with NAV above R$ 500 million and fewer than 5 quotaholders are part of the universe of 4,604. Without separating these two groups, the number does not precisely support any argument.

Opacity risk from curve marking. This is the most relevant risk for the retail quotaholder and the least visible until it materializes. Under normal conditions, the absence of continuous pricing in the secondary market produces the apparent NAV stability that drove the behavioral demand described earlier. Under credit stress conditions, this same absence means the deterioration of underlying assets is not visible on the statement until the moment the administrator is forced to mark to market — due to declared delinquency, restructuring or guarantee execution. The result is the abrupt markdown documented in the 2024 agro delinquency cycle, in which funds with stable NAV recorded drops of 10% to 20% in isolated months. Technically, this is not volatility — it is the collapse of the lag between accounting NAV and the recoverable value of the assets. The secondary market for cetipado quotas amplifies this effect: thin under normal conditions, it can become nonexistent under stress, forcing the quotaholder who needs to exit before maturity to accept significant discounts on the reported NAV. The apparent stability of the cetipado quota is not a property of the asset. It is a property of the pricing methodology.

Platform concentration risk. When a single administrator manages more than 600 closed-end funds for an overlapping client base, a stress event at the administrator — regulatory, operational or reputational — affects formally independent positions simultaneously. This risk does not appear in any individual fund's prospectus and is only measurable at the aggregate level.

Sizing risk. According to CVM's open data, 17.2% of closed-end funds registered in the period have NAV below R$ 10 million. For a FIDC or FIP in that range, fixed structural costs — administration, custody, oversight, audit — consume a relevant portion of gross return before any illiquidity premium is calculated. The net return to quotaholders of these funds, in general, does not compensate for the illiquidity risk assumed.

Allocation criteria: what the professional allocator must verify

The analysis above does not condemn the product. It identifies the conditions under which it is suitable.

There is a methodological warning that precedes any checklist: in cetipado funds, retrospective performance analysis is not due diligence — it is noise with the appearance of signal. Curve marking produces artificially stable historical NAV series. They do not reveal the quality of the underlying portfolio. The monthly statement does not tell the story of risk — it tells the accounting story. These two stories diverge silently until a credit event forces them to converge abruptly.

Due diligence needs to be prospective. The allocator does not analyze what the fund has delivered — it analyzes how the manager originates, selects and monitors assets before any credit event. The questions that distribution materials do not answer:

Liquidity of the overall portfolio. Capital allocated to cetipados should represent a defined, sustainable fraction of real illiquidity in the investor's total portfolio. The question is not "what is the fund's term," but "what is the impact on portfolio liquidity if that capital is unavailable for the maximum stated term."

Verifiable net premium. The premium over the equivalent liquid instrument, calculated after all structure fees — administration, performance, distribution and custody — should be positive and proportional to the risk assumed. In funds with NAV below R$ 100 million, fixed structural costs systematically compress this premium. The calculation should be made, not assumed.

Track record in the specific strategy. The difference between a manager with an auditable track record in the proposed strategy and a manager with two years of existence and growing NAV is information about portfolio behavior in adverse cycles. Fundraising history does not substitute for performance history.

Pricing transparency. In cetipado funds, apparent NAV stability is not evidence of low risk — it is evidence of curve-marking methodology. The allocator should verify: how often and under what conditions does the administrator mark assets to market? How did NAV behave during periods of stress in the segment? Is there a functional secondary market for the quotas, and at what discount?

Manager alignment after fundraising. The quotaholder should verify how the strategy manager maintains exposure to the fund's performance after fundraising closes: direct stake in the vehicle, performance fee calculated on actual return — not on projected IRR — and any lock-up mechanisms applicable to the manager itself. The history of closures and liquidations of the same manager's prior funds is a relevant source of information about this behavior over the cycle.

Summary

The growth of 4,604 new cetipado fund classes between 2023 and 2026 had four converging forces: behavioral demand for instruments without visible volatility on the statement; reduced regulatory cost of creating closed-end vehicles under RCVM 175; an incentive structure in the distribution chain favoring revenue recognition at fundraising; and the elimination of tax deferral in conventional exclusive funds under Law 14,754/2023, which directed the reorganization of high-net-worth wealth toward cetipado structures exempt from come-cotas.

Of this universe, a relevant fraction is made up of wealth governance vehicles and institutional structures, not distribution products for the retail qualified investor. The same regulatory wrapper houses everything from senior FIDCs with documented subordination and auditable portfolios to equity FIPs with no structural guarantee and undersized funds where fixed costs erode the illiquidity premium. The category does not inform the risk.

The illiquidity premium exists. In well-sized structures, with verifiable origination and documented incentive alignment, it is capturable. The problem is not the instrument — it is the selection.

The monthly statement of a cetipado fund does not measure risk. It defers it. The absence of visible volatility is not a property of the asset — it is a property of the pricing method. As long as credit does not deteriorate to the point of forcing a mark to market, the statement will always be correct and never informative.

Selection rigor is the only real mark to market available to the allocator. Confusing statement stability with asset quality is the mistake this market will still collect from many portfolios.

Sources

CVM Open Data: registro_classe.csv and registro_fundo.csv, accessed on April 23, 2026. Scope: funds in Normal Operation, closed-end structure, FII/FIP/FIDC/FIAGRO types, start between January 1, 2023 and April 23, 2026. Total: 4,604 classes. Methodology: matching by administrator/manager CNPJ; adjusted NAV excludes funds with NAV above R$ 50 billion.

ANBIMA: Investment Product Distribution Code, mandatory mark-to-market requirement for private fixed-income securities in effect as of January 2, 2023. Available at anbima.com.br.

Bloomberg Línea, March 8, 2023: "Americanas crisis leads to R$ 66 billion in redemptions in credit funds," citing an Itaú BBA estimate for the period January 12, 2023–March 2, 2023.

ANBIMA: FIDC fundraising in 2024, R$ 81.4 billion, up 86.1% from 2023. Annual Capital Markets Report 2024.

ANBIMA: FIDC NAV, R$ 741.1 billion in the twelve months ended November 2025, up 22.5%. Released in December 2025.

Central Bank of Brazil: historical Selic rate targets, Copom. Available at bcb.gov.br.

CVM Resolution 160: governs public offerings of closed-end fund quotas. CVM Resolution 175: reorganized the regulatory architecture of investment funds, in effect since October 2023. CVM Resolution 204: extended adaptation deadlines to RCVM 175 for existing funds, with a final deadline of December 31, 2024 for most categories; FIDCs had specific transition windows for Annex V.

Law 14,754, of December 12, 2023: institutes semiannual withholding tax (come-cotas) for conventional closed-end funds and taxation of offshore funds and controlled entities. In effect as of January 1, 2024.

Cetipados Fund Radar (XP Asset): July 2025 and December 2025 editions. Authors: Marx Gonçalves and Eduardo Bacelar. Basis for the composition of the 43-fund sample and dividend yield and benchmark data for cetipado FIIs.

Quantum Finance: Fiagros Panorama, November 2025. Available at quantumfinance.com.br. Basis for NAV and returns of cetipado Fiagros.

List of Cetipado Funds (BTG Pactual Asset Management): accessed April 2026. FI-Infra and cetipado private credit data.

Mais Retorno: fund database, accessed April 24, 2026. Used to verify the number of quotaholders and NAV for funds with institutional structures identified in the CVM database.

item.title: Real estate as investment: the premise the data doesn't support
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: Real estate holds a singular position in Brazilian financial culture. It is treated as the store of value par excellence, a tangible asset that withstands crises, generates income, and appreciates over time. This…
item.content:encoded:
Real estate holds a singular position in Brazilian financial culture. It is treated as the store of value par excellence, a tangible asset that withstands crises, generates income, and appreciates over time. This conviction crosses generations and levels of financial sophistication. That is exactly why it deserves rigorous examination.

The premise has legitimate historical roots in a country that experienced hyperinflation, savings confiscation, and chronic monetary instability. The problem is that it survived the context that justified it. Today it operates as bias, not as analysis.

The anatomy of any income-producing asset

Every income-producing asset has two components: a principal, which needs to preserve value over time, and a periodic income, which compensates the capital while it is committed.

With real estate, the principal is the value of the property. What determines its variation is not an inflation index, but variables specific to the real estate market: location, supply and demand, credit availability, interest rate levels, and regional infrastructure. FipeZAP consolidates the outcome of these forces into an observable index — it measures what the market actually practiced, not a correction contractually guaranteed by any index. Rent is the periodic income, paid monthly by the tenant.

The Brazilian capital markets offer an asset class with a superficially similar structure, but with a fundamental difference: federal government bonds linked to the IPCA have their Updated Nominal Value adjusted daily by the official index, by contract, without depending on any market variable. The periodic income is the coupon, paid at a frequency that varies by bond. The entry cost is close to zero.

This distinction is not cosmetic. With real estate, preservation of the principal depends on forces the investor does not control and that bear no direct relationship to inflation. With the NTN-B, correction of the principal is a contractual obligation of the National Treasury, calculated on the official IPCA from IBGE, independent of any market condition. This analysis sets both sides of the equation on the same criteria.

What you pay before you even start

Whoever buys a R$500,000 property commits, in practice, R$542,500.

  • ITBI (3%): R$15,000

  • Brokerage (5%): R$25,000

  • Notary and registration (0.5%): R$2,500

Total entry friction: R$42,500, equivalent to 8.5% of the asset. That money does not earn a return, does not come back, and does not compound. The property starts 8.5% below the starting point before any return is generated. With IPCA-linked government bonds, the entry cost is close to zero.

Source: municipal ITBI tables, average of Brazilian state capitals.

The income that rent actually delivers

FipeZAP points to an annualized residential rental yield of 6.2% in February 2026. On R$500,000, that represents R$31,000 gross per year. That number does not reach the investor's pocket.

Historical average vacancy is 10% of the period. Net of that, effective rent falls to R$27,900. Average property tax (IPTU): 0.5% of value, R$2,500 annually. Conservative maintenance: another 0.5%, R$2,500. The result before income tax is R$22,900 annually, R$1,908 per month. With income tax under the progressive table, estimated effective rate of 15%: another R$3,435 goes out.

  • Net income in the first year: R$19,465, equivalent to R$1,622 per month.

  • Net yield on committed capital (R$542,500): 3.59% per year.

The government bond with semiannual coupons linked to IPCA, traded on April 10, 2026 at IPCA + 7.34%, delivers a tax-free coupon of R$2,125 per month over the same period, with initial capital R$42,500 lower and zero active management. Thirty-one percent more net income from the very first month.

By 2036, with the Updated Nominal Value growing 4.5% per year via IPCA, the bond's monthly net coupon reaches R$3,300. The property's net rent, whose price moved according to the real estate market's own dynamics at a CAGR of 3.5% per year over the last ten years, reaches, after all costs, R$2,288. The bond's advantage increases over time.

Source: FipeZAP — National residential index, Feb. 2026; Tesouro Direto — rates as of April 10, 2026.

The retirement that real estate promises

The second most common use of real estate as an investment is building future income. You buy today to rent out in ten or fifteen years. The Brazilian capital markets have an instrument designed precisely for this: Tesouro Renda+.

Calculation memo — bond for future income (IPCA + 7.11%), 10 years of accumulation:

  • Nominal return: (1 + 7.11%) × (1 + 4.5%) − 1 = 11.93% per year

  • Capital accumulated by 2036: R$500,000 × (1.1193)^10 = R$1,543,239

  • Gross monthly income: R$11,861

  • After 15% income tax: R$10,082/month net, adjusted by IPCA, for 20 years.

An important structural point: Renda+ does not return the principal as a lump sum at the end. Each monthly installment includes real interest plus principal amortization — it is an annuity. At the end of the 240 months, the balance is zero. The total net amount received over the 20 years is R$2,419,740, which incorporates the full return of the accumulated capital of R$1,543,239 plus the real interest of the period.

Real estate under the same conditions delivers in 2036, after vacancy, costs, and income tax, considering that its value evolved according to real estate market variables as consolidated by FipeZAP: R$2,288/month.

Four point four times less monthly income. With active management, vacancy risk, and zero guarantee of cash flow.

Source: Tesouro Direto — Renda+ 2036, rate as of April 10, 2026; FipeZAP — national historical series.

Pure accumulation

For those who don't need income during the period and want to maximize wealth in ten years:

Real estate:

  • Committed capital: R$542,500

  • Net value in 2036: R$674,504 (CAGR of 3.5% p.a., the result of market dynamics via FipeZAP, after income tax).

  • Net accumulated income (10 years): R$194,650

  • Total wealth: R$869,154 | Real IRR: 0.94% per year

Principal government bond (IPCA + 7.11%):

  • Capital: R$500,000

  • Gross value in 2036: R$1,543,239

  • After 15% income tax and B3 custody fees: R$1,374,753 | Real CAGR: 5.88% per year

The bond adjusts the principal daily by IPCA, by contract. Real estate appreciates according to market variables — credit, demand, location, the Selic rate — with no guarantee of outcome whatsoever. Over the last ten years, the result of these variables, as measured by FipeZAP, was 3.5% per year nominal, below inflation for the period.

The final wealth of the investor in the IPCA+ bond is 58% higher, with initial capital R$42,500 lower.

Source: FipeZAP — residential CAGR over the last 10 years, national index; Tesouro Direto — NTN-B Principal 2040, rate as of April 10, 2026.

Summary

Assumptions: IPCA 4.5% per year (top of the target range, consistent with the neutral rate declared by the BCB); real estate CAGR 3.5% nominal (FipeZAP, last 10 years — the result of the real estate market's own dynamics, not IPCA indexation); rental yield 6.2% (FipeZAP, Feb. 2026); government bond rates as of April 10, 2026; 15% income tax in all cases.

What the statement doesn't show

The numbers answer the return. They don't explain why real estate persists as the dominant choice even with a systematic disadvantage in the data. The answer lies in how often the risk is observed.

1. Volatility and the Pain of Loss: Long-term government bonds have high duration. When rates rise, market price falls. In 2024, portfolios with long IPCA+ bonds posted declines of 20% or more. Kahneman and Tversky showed that the pain of a loss is roughly twice the satisfaction of a gain. The investor sees it, feels it, and sells at the worst moment. Real estate does not produce this signal. In 2015-2017, FipeZAP recorded a nominal decline, but no statement ever notified the investor. The risk was present; what differed was the frequency of measurement.

2. The Illusion of Control: The real estate investor feels in control (renovation, rent, tenant). With bonds, the perception is one of passivity in the face of Copom decisions. The illusion of control has real psychological value, but it costs 4.94 percentage points per year in sacrificed real return.

3. Return Risk vs. Exit Risk: A government bond held to maturity has no return risk. Whoever locks in IPCA + 7.11% today and holds the bond receives exactly that. Real estate never offers that guarantee. Its value at sale depends on interest rates, credit, and local dynamics — variables the investor does not control and that FipeZAP only records ex-post.

When real estate makes sense

This analysis does not condemn real estate as an asset class, but it does delimit the context in which it is justified:

  • When there is a local information advantage that the average index does not capture (anticipated demand vectors).

  • Acquisition below market value (auctions, distressed sales, or off-plan purchases with a real discount).

  • Value-add strategies, where the return comes from the ability to add something the market has not yet priced in.

  • When personal use justifies the asset regardless of pure financial return.

The case that does not hold up is the most common one: buying a standard residential property to rent out, convinced that the asset will "track inflation" through some intrinsic property. It won't. The real estate market (credit, interest rates, supply) will determine the outcome. And over the last ten years, that outcome, as consolidated by FipeZAP, came in below the IPCA in real terms.

Choosing real estate with clear-eyed awareness of these numbers is a legitimate decision. Recognizing psychological and inheritance-related factors is different from ignoring the numbers. A conscious choice presupposes knowing the cost of what one is choosing.

Sources:

  • FipeZAP — Residential Property Price Index, national historical series, Jan. 2008 to Mar. 2026 (FIPE/ZAP Imóveis).

  • Tesouro Direto — IPCA+ bond rates, consulted on April 10, 2026.

  • BCB — Focus Report and communications on the structural neutral interest rate.

  • Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk.

  • FipeZAP — April 2025 and December 2024 reports (FIPE/OLX Group).

item.title: Code, Cash Flow, and Forensic Accounting: Using AI Agents to Automate Financial Statement Analysis
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: I've been testing artificial intelligence tools since the first language models became accessible. I've already tried applications focused on text, image, and audio automation. None,…
item.content:encoded:
I've been testing artificial intelligence tools since the first language models became accessible. I've already tried applications focused on text, image, and audio automation. None, however, changed my experimentation routine as much as coding agents.

The idea is simple: you describe the logic and the agent produces functional code. This substantially shifts the boundary of what's possible for someone who understands the problem, but isn't a professional developer.

Integrating quantitative finance and AI

While studying Evaluating the Quality of Financial Reports in preparation for CFA Level II, I decided to combine two vectors:

  • Classic forensic accounting models

  • AI agents specialized in code automation

The question guiding the experiment was straightforward:

Given that the models, metrics, and validation criteria are known, to what extent can an AI agent build a functional system autonomously?

The prototype: Advisor-Brain-FSA

The result was Advisor-Brain-FSA, a prototype that automatically runs:

  • Beneish M-Score

  • Accruals Quality framework

Applied to public CVM data, with a full pipeline of ingestion, transformation, calculation, and visualization. The website represents only the visual product of the experiment.

Experiment output: https://evaluating-quality-of-financial-reports-production.up.railway.app

The main lesson was not in code generation, but in the points where the agent fails structurally without human intervention guided by technical domain knowledge.

What was automated and the limits encountered

Experiment premise: Implement the Beneish M-Score (1999) and accruals quality metrics using CVM data, letting the agent build the entire pipeline.

Objective: Identify quantitative signals of:

  • Inflated revenue recognition

  • Inappropriate expense capitalization

  • Divergence between accounting profit and operating cash flow

Three central limitations emerged.

1. Sector applicability of the model

The first failure was trying to apply the Beneish M-Score indiscriminately to the more than 420 listed companies.

The model assumes the existence of accounts such as:

  • Cost of Goods Sold

  • Inventories

These accounts don't exist in the accounting structure of banks, insurers, and financial institutions. Unrestricted application generates severe distortions and false positives.

The solution required a conceptual decision: instructing the agent to build a sector filter, excluding financial institutions based on the CVM registry and applying the model only to roughly 260 companies in the real sector.

The agent fully implemented the logic. Defining the scope was human.

2. Sign convention in CVM data

In CVM data, expense accounts — such as Depreciation — are provided with a negative sign. Without an explicit absolute value adjustment, the DEPI (Depreciation Index) ends up distorting the M-Score.

This is a relevant limit of current agents: they replicate formulas with syntactic precision, but they don't understand accounting conventions implicit in the data.

To identify the problem, an additional Year-over-Year visualization layer was needed, displaying the intermediate accounting values before the indices were calculated. This is domain knowledge that doesn't emerge from the formula.

3. Backtest with restated financial statements (CVCB3)

For validation, the engine was tested on CVC in 2019, the year in which fraud related to revenue recognition and expense capitalization was acknowledged.

The M-Score didn't flag a failure. The reason is structural: the data currently made available by CVM corresponds to the restated financial statements, already corrected after the audit. The original data is no longer available.

Even so, the model captured relevant changes in the Asset Quality Index (AQI) resulting from the restatement. This indicates that partial anomalies can be detected even in corrected datasets, but it imposes a clear limitation on any attempt at rigorous historical backtesting.

Applied test: Ambipar (AMBP3)

Forensic accounting isn't limited to fraud detection. It is, above all, a tool for assessing earnings quality.

In the test with Ambipar (2023), the system indicated:

  • M-Score below the formal "manipulator" threshold

  • Relevant alerts in the DSRI (receivables growing faster than revenue) and SGI indices

The automatic interpretation layer reclassified the result as Grade C – Questionable Quality, indicating the need for greater scrutiny of credit and growth policies.

This is the same signal that careful Equity Research work would raise, with a significant difference in time and operating cost.

Conclusions from the experiment

The prototype evolved from local execution to persistent cloud cache to address memory limitations. Not a single line of code was written directly by me:

  • The agent built the implementation

  • The architecture, validation, and conceptual corrections were human

The pattern observed is consistent:

  • Agents are highly effective at structure, syntax, and automation

  • They systematically fail at aspects requiring accounting, regulatory, and methodological context

The agent doesn't know that:

  • Banks don't have inventory

  • CVM uses a negative sign for expenses

  • Restated financial statements compromise historical backtests

For professionals with technical domain expertise, translating field knowledge into precise instructions for AI agents is today the most efficient way to understand where this technology actually adds value — and where it still depends entirely on human judgment.

Legal and Regulatory Disclaimer

Advisor-Brain-FSA is a research experiment in data automation and artificial intelligence, based on quantitative methodologies studied at the CFA Institute.

The results presented (M-Score, Accrual Ratio, and heuristic narratives):

  • Are derived from automated processing of public CVM data

  • Do not constitute investment recommendations, fiduciary advice, or an offer of securities

  • Do not replace independent analysis, audit, or professional due diligence

Quantitative indicators assess probabilities and statistical inconsistencies, and do not replace sound analytical judgment.

item.title: The US-Iran War Is a Game of Chicken. And Brazil Is at the Table, Like It or Not.
item.dc:creator: Alisson Prata
item.description: I'll be direct: the February 28 bombing changed the geopolitical chessboard irreversibly. The decapitation of Ayatollah Khamenei and the succession by Mojtaba Khamenei under jihad rhetoric…
item.content:encoded:
I'll be direct: the February 28 bombing changed the geopolitical chessboard irreversibly. The decapitation of Ayatollah Khamenei and the succession by Mojtaba Khamenei under jihad rhetoric turned what was strategic tension into a war of national survival. This isn't a headline. It's a macroeconomic variable.

And most of the Brazilian market is still looking at IPCA as if it were a domestic problem.

It isn't. It's an exogenous shock with direct transmission.

I spend a good part of my time on risk models and stress scenarios. And what caught my attention in this crisis wasn't oil going up. That's obvious. What caught my attention was the structure of the game.

Anyone who's studied Thomas Schelling knows: what's happening between the US/Israel and Iran is a classic Game of Chicken. Two players accelerating toward each other. Whoever swerves first loses credibility. Whoever doesn't swerve might die.

The Nash Equilibrium here isn't peace. It's prolonged, high-intensity friction. And that changes everything for anyone pricing assets.

For Iran, swerving means losing regional hegemony and strategic relevance. For the US, swerving means admitting its security architecture in the Middle East is obsolete. Neither side can swerve without an unacceptable political cost. So the game continues.

And this is where the concept that interests me most as an engineer by training comes in: cost asymmetry.

An Iranian Shahed drone costs between US$30,000 and US$50,000. A Patriot interceptor costs US$4 million per shot. Iran is operating with negative convexity over the Western defense budget. Every cheap attack forces an expensive response. This isn't terrorism. It's economic engineering of attrition.

And the Strait of Hormuz, through which 21% of the world's oil transits, is the lever. It's the collateral.

Now let's get to what matters for anyone investing in Brazil.

The Treasury's Technical Note from March 2026 puts the numbers on the table. Comparing the February base scenario with the disruptive shock scenario (Brent at US$100):

Brent: from US$65.97 to US$100.00. A 51.5% increase.

GDP: from 2.30% to 2.66%. Up 0.36 p.p.

IPCA: from 3.60% to 4.28%. Up 0.68 p.p.

IGP-DI: from 4.60% to 4.90%.

Additional trade surplus: +US$10.3 billion.

Additional net tax revenue: +R$96.6 billion.

Read these numbers carefully.

Brazil gains R$96.6 billion in extra fiscal revenue with high oil prices. GDP rises. The trade surplus expands. Sounds great, right?

Not so fast.

IPCA goes to 4.28%, pressuring the ceiling of the target. IGP-DI jumps because of the extractive industry and nitrogen fertilizers. Household debt is already at 80.2%, which means any cost pass-through at the pump compresses real consumption. And capital flight toward US Treasuries pressures the exchange rate and risk premiums on our assets.

This is Brazil's dilemma: we're net oil exporters, but importers of stability. The commodity's appreciation enriches the State and impoverishes the household. It's an internal asymmetry that mirrors the asymmetry of the conflict abroad.

The government's response came via Provisional Measure (MP) 1,340/2026. There are three mechanisms:

A subsidy of R$0.32 per liter of road diesel, capped at R$10 billion. A 12% Export Tax on crude oil (NCM 2709). A 50% Export Tax on diesel (NCM 2710.19.21) for as long as the subsidy lasts.

In practice, the MP transfers part of the export surplus to contain the pass-through of the shock to domestic fuel prices. The direct target is diesel, which is the base cost of agricultural freight. The projected harvest of 344.1 million tons depends on viable shipping. If diesel rises without a cushion, the freight cost contaminates the agro-export chain and food inflation accelerates.

Penalties for abusive price increases across the distribution chain were recalibrated to a range of R$50,000 to R$500 million (Law No. 9,847/1999).

The net effect of the MP is still open. Its effectiveness depends on the duration of the conflict, distributor compliance, and exchange rate behavior. These are variables no model controls precisely at this moment.

But the central point I want to leave you with isn't about the crisis. It's about what comes next.

R$96.6 billion in additional fiscal revenue is a significant volume. The question that imposes itself is: where does that money go?

Brazil has known structural bottlenecks that this bonus could address or ignore:

First, refining and storage. The country is a net oil exporter, but remains exposed to derivatives market volatility due to insufficient refining capacity.

Second, nitrogen fertilizers. The 344 million ton harvest depends on imported inputs, some of them originating in the Middle East. Any prolonged disruption to Persian Gulf routes is a direct risk to agricultural productivity.

Third, logistical concentration. Dependence on chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz is a systemic vulnerability factor for any economy that depends on global trade.

Sérgio Botton Barcellos frames the issue precisely: national sovereignty in times of crisis is measured by the ability to combine control over energy vectors with long-term state policies. A country that exports raw commodities and imports derivatives remains vulnerable to the power cycles of major powers.

A State's ability to navigate asymmetric shocks without disintegrating its social fabric or its productive base is what will define positions in the new international order.

The US-Iran conflict isn't just a war. It's a stress test for every economic model that depends on global chains.

Brazil has a fiscal window opened by the shock. What's done with it will determine whether the country emerges from this crisis with more structural resilience or just a one-off surplus.

This is the kind of variable that doesn't show up in any model, but defines long-term trajectories.
